More than two years after West Palm Beach native Virgil Price III disappeared during a freedive and never resurfaced on Mother's Day morning, his family finally has a place to visit, remember him and find a measure of peace.On Thursday, loved ones gathered off the coast of Palm Beach County as a memorial reef sculpted in Price's image was deployed into the Atlantic Ocean, creating a permanent tribute to the 39-year-old diver whose passion for the ocean shaped his life.WATCH: Memorial reef offers closure for family of missing freediverFor Price's family, who never recovered his body, the project represents far more than an artificial reef. It's a permanent place of remembrance and a source of closure after years of grief."It's just very emotional," said his mother, Kate Cerasaro. "Really happy to think Virgil will finally have a resting place since we never found his body."Price disappeared during a Mother's Day dive in 2024 and never resurfaced; that was the last time Cerasaro spoke with her son.WPTV has been connected with the family ever since his disappearance.Family members described him as a lifelong ocean lover, athlete, musician and conservation advocate. They said he volunteered at Loggerhead Marinelife Center as a teenager and later spent time in Trinidad and Tobago teaching at-risk youth how to swim and dive. Family also said he was preparing to compete in the Freediving World Championships in Greece before his disappearance.His younger sister, Brit Drozda, previously told WPTV about her brother's connection to the water."He had such a passion from a young age for the ocean. He taught me how to surf," Drozda said.The memorial reef reflects many of the things that made Virgil who he was.The structure features Virgil making a shaka hand gesture alongside his two beloved dogs. A turtle is included as a nod to his first tattoo and the childhood nickname "Turtle Boy." The design also incorporates a pirate ship representing his childhood imagination, and owls, which he collected.The reef also honors one of his lifelong passions: the ocean."What do you think Virgil would say to know that he's going to have his own little reef built after him?" WPTV asked Cerasaro."I think he would be really excited because he didn't really like attention; he was a musician, he was every other thing, but he never wanted to be the center of attention," answered Cerasaro, who threw up the shaka hand gesture.Built by Reef Cells, the artificial reef is made from 100% ocean-friendly concrete and limestone and weighs approximately six tons. The company also donated additional reef structures that were installed alongside Virgil's reef.The six-ton memorial reef now rests offshore at 26° 45.237' N, 80° 01.584' W, giving Virgil's loved ones a specific place to visit and remember him, even though his body was never recovered.The significance of having a physical place to honor Virgil has been a recurring theme throughout the family's healing process.During a 2025 interview with WPTV while fundraising for the reef project, family unveiled plans for the memorial reef, hoping to create something that reflected Virgil's passion for the ocean and marine conservation."I think he would just love it, I just think it's so Virgil," Cerasaro told WPTV in 2025. "To have fish swimming in and out of it and all around there and adding something to the ecosystem is just what he would love."Now that the reef has been installed, she says that vision has become reality."I just couldn’t believe it, I just burst out crying," said Cerasaro. "I feel like he's surrounded by everything that he loved."For Drozda, watching the deployment brought a sense of peace."I can't wait to see what sea life flourishes down there," said Drozda. "And it's really close to where he used to go surfing and dove himself."She said seeing the memorial on the ocean floor feels fitting because so much of Virgil's life revolved around the water."The piece of peace I have is he was doing something he was so passionate about and loved so much. So to see him in his element and preserved that way is pretty awesome."The project has also been supported in part by Underwater Hypoxic Blackout Prevention, a nonprofit organization dedicated to raising awareness about the condition.The family said they raised approximately $250,000 for the project. About $60,000 to $70,000 of that funding will go back to the nonprofit to support education efforts focused on underwater hypoxic blackout and the dangers of breath-holding underwater.Family members believe underwater hypoxic blackout played a role in Virgil's disappearance. The condition occurs when a swimmer or diver loses consciousness underwater because of a lack of oxygen, often with few visible warning signs.The family's advocacy efforts stem from a desire to prevent other families from experiencing the same tragedy."We've been in touch with a lot of the families who have also lost children like Virgil, and we've become kind of a group that is supporting one another and trying to do something and change some of the regulations," Cerasaro said.In previous interviews with WPTV, Virgil's father, Virgil Price II, also called for additional safety measures within the freediving community, including stronger safeguards and increased awareness about blackout risks.Despite the heartbreak, family members say Virgil's legacy continues to live on through the people he inspired.In a previous WPTV interview, Drozda described the way her brother encouraged others."He was always more excited to see someone conquer their goals and catch their fish than he was for himself," Drozda said.For his loved ones, the reef ensures that legacy will continue beneath the waves, creating habitat for marine life while providing a place where family and friends can honor his memory for years to come.During WPTV's coverage of the family's memorial service in 2024, Cerasaro recalled one of the final conversations she had with her son on Mother's Day morning."He goes, 'Mom, I just want you to know something. You are my inspiration in life. You taught me to look at the underside of the leaf. You taught me to look under the water. You taught me how to laugh at myself. You were my inspiration in life, and when I go down in the water, the first thing I do is say a prayer,'" Cerasaro said.Now, with the reef installed, the family says they have a permanent place to remember the man who loved the ocean more than anything.When asked what she would say if she could share one more message with her son, Cerasaro fought back tears."I love you so much, and I miss you more than you can ever know," Cerasaro said.Moments later, Drozda shared a message of her own."I love you, and I miss you so freaking much," Drozda said.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Authorities have not released additional details about the source of the email threat. Parents were notified of the situation through a message from the school Thursday afternoon. No evidence of threat found In an update issued at 2:55 p.m., school officials said the Martin County Sheriff's Office was finalizing its sweep of the campus and found no evidence of a threat. A new water-management project in Martin County is expected to redirect billions of gallons of water away from the St. Lucie Estuary, helping reduce the risk of harmful algal blooms. Ron DeSantis joined state environmental officials in Palm City on Wednesday to mark the completion of the C-23 Estuary Discharge Diversion Project . The project includes nearly seven miles of new canal and a pump station that will redirect excess water from the C-23 Canal to the C-44 reservoir and stormwater treatment area. There, the water can be stored and cleaned instead of flowing directly into the St. This is yet another tool to manage water before it reaches the estuary, DeSantis said. It will, of course, allow us to further the reduction of harmful discharges and algal blooms within the St. The system entered operational testing in May and has already diverted nearly 5 billion gallons of water, according to DeSantis. Drew Bartlett, executive director of the South Florida Water Management District , said the pump station can move as much as 166 million gallons of water per day. It has worked since May 14, Bartlett said. I looked at the water quality data. Historically, excess water from the C-23 Canal was routed toward the South Fork of the St. Those freshwater flows can disrupt the estuary’s natural salinity balance while carrying nutrients that contribute to algae growth. Florida Department of Environmental Protection Secretary Alexis Lambert said the completed project is expected to divert 6.3 billion gallons of water from the St. She said it is also projected to prevent an average of 55,000 pounds of nitrogen and 14,000 pounds of phosphorus from entering the river each year. A more natural salinity gradient and better conditions for the estuary will produce better results for residents, for visitors, for business owners all along the Indian River Lagoon, DeSantis said. Lucie County moves ahead on bulk water agreement for P1 Motor private racetrack club The St. Lucie River and Indian River Lagoon suffered widespread toxic algae outbreaks in 2016 and 2018. The blooms damaged wildlife habitat, hurt local businesses and kept residents away from affected waterways. State officials said the new diversion system should help move conditions in the estuary closer to their natural pattern. The project is part of a broader network of restoration efforts involving the St. Lucie River, Indian River Lagoon and Everglades. The South Florida Water Management District and U.S. Army Corps of Engineers also recently marked the completion of construction on the C-23/C-24 Stormwater Treatment Area , which is designed to remove nutrients from water before it reaches the estuary and southern Indian River Lagoon. DeSantis said Florida has committed nearly $10 billion to Everglades restoration and water-quality projects since he took office in 2019. His administration has completed or begun work on more than 90 Everglades-related projects, he said. The governor also discussed the Everglades Agricultural Area Reservoir south of Lake Okeechobee . DeSantis said a state and federal agreement is expected to accelerate that project’s completion from 2034 to 2029. Once completed, the EAA reservoir is designed to store water from Lake Okeechobee, clean it and send it south toward the Everglades and Florida Bay rather than releasing it east into the St. Lucie River or west into the Caloosahatchee River.

Fort Pierce police officers can no longer run a license plate through the department's Flock camera system on their own. That power now sits with a handful of people at the top of the department, one of several new restrictions Chief David Smith rolled out this week after a former officer was arrested and accused of using the system to search for a woman he once dated 382 times. "The cameras are here for our community's safety, not to be abused by those who were entrusted to safeguard them," Smith said. Under the new rules, every use of the license plate reader system requires sign off from one of the department's two deputy chiefs before a search is run. Only lieutenants and above can access the system at all. Every query must be tied to a case number, and the system can only be used in two situations: investigations of forcible felonies as defined under Florida law, and cases involving missing or endangered people. "The system will not be used for general investigative surveillance, intelligence gathering unrelated to an authorized investigation, or routine investigative inquiries," Smith said. See also: Argument ends in stabbing; victim flees to West Palm Beach fire station, attacked again The department is also holding onto far less of the data it collects. Smith said Flock camera records are now deleted after 7 days instead of 30. Smith laid out how the process works on the ground. If detectives at a shooting or other serious scene believe the cameras could help, the lieutenant on scene calls one of the two deputy chiefs and explains what they want to search and why. "If they receive approval, then that lieutenant would be the one to do the query for that information. And that would require a case number specifically tied to an investigation," Smith said. Before this change, individual officers and detectives had their own user access and could search the system directly. Smith also created a new position in the department's Office of Professional Standards to conduct monthly quality assurance audits of every law enforcement database officers use, not just Flock. "Accountability requires meaningful controls, supervision, and verification," Smith said. While some people who spoke to CBS12 News are happy about the changes, some say they're conflicted about Flock camera use at all. You know, we do have we do have our own rights, you know, and all this data collection and everything else is definitely infringing upon that. On the other side of it, it is a great tool for law enforcement," said Edward Smith. "I think it's a good thing that they crack down on it. Like, you don't have to have it. You know, I don't need a camera watching me walk into the bathroom." Smith said he started reviewing the department's technology policies after becoming chief in February and had already begun a one-year audit of database usage before the media brought the allegations against former officer Josepher Crutchfield to the department in August. But he said the deputy chief approval and lieutenant-only access rules were added after that investigation began. Smith declined to give a specific date for when the earlier changes took effect, saying it was roughly two months ago. "This case demonstrates that the safeguards that were in place were not sufficient," Smith said. "What we learned through this investigation reinforced the need for the changes that were already underway, and it made clear that we needed to go significantly further, and we have." Crutchfield was arrested Tuesday on four felony counts of unauthorized computer access and was being held at the St. Lucie County Jail on an $80,000 bond. Police say he searched the same license plate 382 times between October 2025 and July 2026, most of the time while off duty, and that the plate belonged to a woman he had dated. Investigators say he also searched for her in the FCIC, NCIC, DAVID and TLO databases, some of that going back to 2023. He resigned in August before the investigation concluded. When asked whether that many searches on a single plate should have raised alarms sooner, Smith said the department's audit was already working backward month by month when the media tip came in. "It's definitely unusual activity when you've got somebody doing multiple single point searches on a license plate," Smith said. "I do believe that we would have gotten there and we would have identified these." The department's broader audit is still ongoing. Smith said no additional violations have been found so far. The new rules land as Fort Pierce is also pulling cameras off the road. Smith said the department will comply with a recent Florida Department of Transportation directive and the St. Lucie County Commission's directive covering license plate readers on state and county rights-of-way. He estimated about 50 cameras will come down, leaving roughly 20 on city roads. He said the department is still working on a removal plan and it will take time. Smith defended the technology even as he restricted it, saying the cameras were integral to solving every homicide the city has closed recently and to identifying the driver in the hit-and-run that seriously injured a seven-year-old girl. I understand why people are having that discussion about the use of Flock systems. But it is an immensely useful tool to law enforcement," Smith said.

Florida’s race for governor is becoming a fight over who’s too extreme and who’s too connected.Republican nominee Byron Donalds is portraying Democrat David Jolly as an ally of socialism. Jolly and fellow Democrats are countering with attacks on Republican donors, President Donald Trump’s policies and the cost of living.The competing pitches are arriving just as voters typically begin paying closer attention, according to political analyst Susan MacManus.At the GOP’s midterm convention in Dallas on Wednesday, Donalds accused Jolly of embracing “radical socialism.”“This election cycle is about one thing: common sense versus crazy,” Donalds said.He singled out Jolly’s proposal for public hurricane coverage, describing it as a government takeover of property insurance and warning it would leave Floridians paying a new tax. Donalds argued the costs would reach beyond coastal homeowners to renters and other insurance customers.Donalds also credited Republican tax and regulatory policies with Florida’s economic growth and blamed Democrats for rising costs.The ideological theme continued Thursday at Miami’s Bay of Pigs Museum, where Gov. Ron DeSantis promoted classroom lessons about the dangers of communism.Donalds’ running mate, former state Sen. Bryan Avila, joined DeSantis and accused Democrats of promoting socialist policies. Avila invoked his family’s experience fleeing communist Cuba.“In fact, I’ve offered several of them to give them a one-way trip to Cuba, so that they understand the horrors of communism,” Avila said.The Republican attacks also extend to state Rep. Angie Nixon, the Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate, whose association with the Democratic Socialists of America has become a campaign issue.Nixon joined the organization in June, according to PolitiFact’s reporting published by WLRN. The group advocates replacing capitalism with democratic socialism and collective ownership of major industries.Nixon has rejected the socialist label, saying she joined over shared priorities such as universal health care. Axios reported her explanation.“The right-wing machine is going to do everything that they can to attack us and take our eyes off the fact that we deserve health care, we deserve access to quality public schools,” Nixon said in a recent podcast appearance.Democrats are trying to turn the conversation back to household budgets and Republican leadership.During a virtual news conference Wednesday, Florida Democratic Party Chair Nikki Fried accused Donalds of supporting Trump’s policies at Floridians’ expense.“Let me be clear: there is nothing about this record that is worth celebrating,” Fried said.Jolly’s attack follows the money. He alleged that donors supporting Donalds expect influence in return.“The same people that have owned Tallahassee for 30 years are buying Byron right now, because they want to control Tallahassee, not because they care about Byron,” Jolly said in an online video.Jolly framed his campaign as a chance to disrupt that power, arguing that a coalition seeking change could overcome Donalds’ financial advantage.MacManus said the period after Labor Day has long marked a turning point in voter attention. Campaigns time their strongest messages to when people are preparing to cast ballots, she said.“There’s an old saying that you save your best ads and strategies for right at the point when people actually begin casting ballots,” MacManus said.But getting voters’ attention is only part of the challenge. Distrust of politics and lower participation in midterm elections make turnout difficult, she said. Liking an ad or favoring a candidate in a poll does not guarantee someone will vote.“The game is absolutely turnout,” MacManus said.For both parties, the test is whether the attacks translate into votes.

Indian River County deputies arrested two men in separate cases involving alleged illegal saw palmetto berry harvesting over the Labor Day weekend, according to arrest affidavits. Corey Michael Smith, of Vero Beach, was arrested Sept. 4 after deputies responded to a trespassing call at a BP gas station on 9th Street Southwest, the affidavit states. A deputy said a helicopter crew had spotted Smith on Indian River County School Board property near 800 20th Ave. Deputies found him at the gas station with five black bags containing saw palmetto stalks, according to the affidavit. Smith allegedly showed deputies a palmetto berry harvesting permit that listed an address on 17th Avenue Southwest. The affidavit says the property owner told deputies Smith did not have permission to harvest on the property, which belongs to the Salvation Army . Smith was arrested on charges of using a false or forged palmetto berry harvest permit, disclosing police radio information to aid a suspect, and trespassing after a warning. The affidavit states a deputy heard dispatch traffic coming from a scanner app on Smith’s phone while he was detained. A day later, deputies arrested Francis Ostrowski after a sheriff’s office camera in the North County Conservation Area near 7800 130th St. captured a man carrying a bag filled with saw palmetto berries, according to his affidavit. See also: South Florida crypto kingpin pleads guilty in alleged $245M theft conspiracy Deputies located Ostrowski nearby with a bag of berries and asked whether he had a permit to harvest them. Ostrowski said he did not, the affidavit states. Ostrowski was arrested on a felony charge of harvesting an endangered plant without a permit. The arrests come amid a series of recent saw palmetto berry cases across the Treasure Coast. CBS12 previously reported on arrests involving the alleged theft of about 200 pounds of berries in Martin County and about 150 pounds in Indian River County . In another recent case, a Boynton Beach man was arrested after deputies said they found about 500 pounds of saw palmetto berries .

Every fall, at the start of the school year, a Port St. Lucie social studies teacher takes her students back to a day they never lived through.WATCH BELOW: 'They deserved to be remembered. Their legacy deserves to be carried on,' Ayleen Charles tells WPTV's Zitlali SolacheAyleen Charles has been teaching for over a decade. Each year, she makes Sept. 11 a centerpiece of her classroom."It's important to keep that memory alive, because that what history is right?" Charles said.Charles said her students have only ever known a world shaped by the attacks."You were born in a world shaped by 9/11. They don't know what it's like to be in a world that was not shaped by 9/11," Charles said.To make the history feel real, she uses survivor stories, images and audio recordings — including firsthand accounts from those who were there."I let them read first hand accounts of voicemails that were left from people on the airplane. "I want to them to remember how that impacted the people that they know and the world that they currently live in today."For Charles, the mission is personal — and urgent."People deserved to be remembered. Two boat clubs with locations on the Treasure Coas t have shut down within days of each other, leaving local members without access to boats they paid thousands of dollars to use. Both companies also operate, or operated, in other parts of Florida. Carefree Boat Club , which had Treasure Coast locations in Fort Pierce, Stuart and Vero Beach, announced Sept. 9 that it had ceased operations across its Treasure Coast, Gulf Coast and North Florida clubs. Donald Charles, a Carefree member, told CBS12 in a phone interview that he got no warning before the shutdown. The only word he received came after the fact, in an email from the company informing members the decision was already final. "This is not a decision we arrived at quickly or willingly," the company wrote in the email Charles shared with CBS12. "The cumulative effects of inflation, sharply higher costs for boats, financing, insurance, dockage, labor, maintenance and repairs, together with softer consumer demand and price sensitivity, severe weather-related disruptions and declining marine asset values, created pressures that ultimately proved unsustainable." The email said all future month-to-month billing had been suspended, but it did not address refunds for members who were charged after their local club stopped operating. JetRide Boat Club , which has a Treasure Coast location in Stuart along with locations elsewhere in Florida, including Englewood, Punta Gorda and the Tampa Bay area, also ceased operations effective Sept. A notice posted to the company's website tells members the closure is permanent. It directs members with questions to email the company directly. Members of both clubs say they are still waiting to hear whether they will get any money back. CBS12 has reached out to both companies for comment and will update this story with their responses.

A new housing development in Palm Springs is aiming to give veterans in Palm Beach County more than just a place to live — it's designed to create stability, support and community.Stand Down PBC is building the "Village of Valor," a veteran-focused neighborhood that will include 54 affordable housing units and on-site support services for veterans and their families.Casino NightOn Nov. 7, Stand Down is hosting Casino Night at the Lake Pavilion in West Palm Beach at 6 p.m. Proceeds will fuel their mission.The project is being led by FaithHopeLove Charity Inc., also known as Stand Down, an organization founded by veteran Roy Foster."When I was released from the military in the '80s, for the next five years or so, I just drifted around and around, not realizing that I actually needed some assistance," Foster said.Foster said his experiences after leaving the military inspired him to create Stand Down after realizing how few services were available for veterans transitioning back into civilian life."I went into the VA in Miami in '89, and the realization of what was available to veterans was frightening," Foster said. "It was a situation where this can't continue to go on and on and on."Foster said the aftermath of the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks further motivated him to dedicate himself full time to helping veterans."I saw the towers being hit," Foster said. "The realization was, I know what happened after Vietnam — limited services, angry veterans coming home. It couldn't continue."He said the goal now is to empower veterans rather than abandon them.Village of Valor to include affordable housing for veteransJosh Maddock, executive director of Stand Down PBC, said the Village of Valor is designed specifically to address affordable housing needs for veterans in Palm Beach County."The Village of Valor is 54 two- and three-bedroom units for our veterans," Maddock said. "It's 130 bedrooms of affordable housing in Palm Beach County."The community is being built for homeless and nearly homeless veterans and their families. Organizers say the site will also include support resources designed to help veterans build long-term stability.The project has personal meaning for many connected to the organization.Board member Sylvia Meade said seeing her husband struggle after military service showed her how important a resource like this can be."After seeing that my husband went through a moment of crisis after being in the Army, having something like this would have been such an amazing resource," Meade said.Veterans share success stories through Stand DownSeveral veterans who received support through Stand Down said transitional housing and assistance programs helped them rebuild their lives.Ariana Valentin said the organization helped her move from renting to homeownership."I'm now a homeowner from being a renter to now a homeowner," Valentin said. "Stand Down was a great resource for me."Veteran and caregiver James McFadden also credited the nonprofit for helping him achieve homeownership."I finally own my home, my first home in April," McFadden said. "I really appreciate Stand Down for helping me to do that."According to Stand Down, the organization provides more than 10,000 sheltered nights annually through Stand Down House and assists more than 1,000 veterans and family members each year through the First Stop Veterans' Resource Center.Construction on the Village of Valor began in late 2025, and organizers say the project represents a long-term effort to reduce veteran homelessness in Palm Beach County.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Ben Shelton had gone toe-to-toe with Carlos Alcaraz for five exhausting sets and finally at 3:33 a.m. Wednesday came the chance to end the U.S. Open champion's title reign.Shelton fired an ace at 146 mph, a ball that Alcaraz couldn't have gotten back even with fresh legs.That gave Shelton a 6-7 (5), 6-1, 6-3, 1-6, 7-6 (10-7) victory in a marathon tussle that was the latest-finishing match in U.S. It was a war,” Shelton said. “Carlos is one of the greatest champions of our sport. It was the most enjoyable match I've had in my career, for sure.”Alcaraz had his 18-match winning streak in Grand Slam tournaments ended in a match that lasted 4 hours, 28 minutes, after he fought deep into the night and early into the next morning in a bid to get his hands on the trophy again.RELATED STORY | Serena Williams makes winning return to professional tennis“I mean it was close, it was really close, so I was disappointed I didn't get the win at the end,” the No. “But I’m happy, I am proud of myself about how I fought. As I said, physically I was really tired but I found a way to push myself.”Shelton next plays No. 11 seed Frances Tiafoe, who kept coming back until he had reached his third U.S. Open semifinal, beating Alex Michelsen 5-7, 3-6, 7-5, 6-3, 7-6 (10-6) on Tuesday.The U.S. is guaranteed to have a representative in Sunday's final as it seeks its first men's major title since Andy Roddick lifted the title here in 2003.Alcaraz had played in the previous latest finish at the U.S. Open when he outlasted Jannik Sinner in a match that finished at 2:50 a.m. in the 2022 quarterfinals en route to his first Grand Slam title at 19.Fans love the energy of a night matchThe U.S. Open craves its night matches and players love the energy the fans provide — even when a number of matches have already gone past 2 a.m. this year.Thousands stayed to the end, with Arthur Ashe Stadium perhaps still one-third full for the finish. Shelton benefited from a home-crowd boost even against the popular Alcaraz, with fans chanting his name along with “USA! USA!”RELATED STORY | WTA introduces gene testing for all players on women's tennis tour“It’s incredible," Shelton said. “I always say that this is the greatest sports city in the world, I say that this is the greatest stadium in the world. I’m just hoping that my best friend and my sister over there don’t have to be at work at 6 a.m. in three hours.”Three of the four singles quarterfinals went to match tiebreakers on a marathon day, which started with Aryna Sabalenka edging Wimbledon champion Linda Noskova to keep her hopes alive of a third straight U.S. Open title.Alcaraz will have to wait for his next one.Instead it was Shelton reaching his third major semifinal, having gotten to the final four in the 2023 U.S. Open and 2025 Australian Open.He seized control by winning nine straight games from early in the second set until he had a 3-0 lead in the third. But Alcaraz, in his first tournament since April after returning from a right wrist injury, battled back even as he vomited before the start of the final set.Alcaraz ran off four straight points in the tiebreaker to go ahead 5-3, but Shelton came back behind some of his powerful serves that can exceed 140 mph, along with some mistakes from Alcaraz. Shelton eventually finished it off with a 146 mph serve his opponent couldn't get back.Alcaraz is now 15-2 in five-set matches. He won his seventh Grand Slam title at the Australian Open to start this year not long before his injury, and came to Flushing Meadows saying he didn't know what to expect.‘I leave with my head held high’“I’m leaving happy and my head held high,” Alcaraz said. “The truth is, I wanted to win ... but also our goal was to leave the tournament having played matches and staying healthy.”Tiafoe reached the semifinals in 2022 and lost to Alcaraz, when the Spaniard won his first of seven Grand Slam titles. Tiafoe lost to fellow American Taylor Fritz two years later, when the U.S. came closest to ending it’s men’s drought.It certainly didn’t appear Tiafoe would be going back this time, after Michelsen continued his dominant run through his breakout tournament. He was the only man who hadn’t dropped a set, and he served to win the match with a 5-4 lead in the third.He couldn't finish it off and Tiafoe charged back after falling behind 3-0 in the fifth set.Tiafoe said his performance to start the match was slow and flat.“It wasn’t good, let’s put it that way. “Three out of five is a blessing, because you have time to get it together. I definitely waited for the last minute.”Tiafoe joined Andre Agassi as the only American men to reach three U.S. Open semifinals this century and will return to the top 10 for the first time in three years in the next rankings.Michelsen, ranked No. 46, fell to 0-6 in matches that go to a fifth set.

Ron DeSantis on Wednesday celebrated the completion of the C-23 Canal Estuary Discharge Diversion Project in Martin County, calling it part of the largest environmental restoration effort in U.S. history.The project, located at 10297 Southwest Martin Highway, will reroute excess water from the C-23 Canal away from the South Fork of the Saint Lucie River — where it had previously contributed to harmful algal blooms — and instead send it through a nearly 7-mile interconnect canal to the C-44 Reservoir and Stormwater Treatment Area.DeSantis was joined at the ribbon-cutting by Florida Department of Environmental Protection Secretary Alexis Lambert and South Florida Water Management District Executive Director Drew Bartlett, along with district board members Chairman Goss, Ronnie Bergeron, Ben Butler, Charlotte Roman, Tom Hurley and Robert Spotswood Jr.Since entering its operational testing phase in May, the project has diverted nearly 5 billion gallons of water away from the Saint Lucie Estuary. When operating at full capacity, the pump stations can fill an Olympic-size swimming pool in just under 6 minutes.Lambert said the project is projected to prevent 55,000 pounds of nitrogen and 14,000 pounds of phosphorus from entering the Saint Lucie River on average each year, and will divert 6.3 billion gallons of water from the river to the C-44 Reservoir and Stormwater Treatment Area."Florida's waterways are a deeply interconnected system and preventing these harmful discharges will further improve the health of the estuary and the lagoon," Lambert said.DeSantis said his administration has invested close to $10 billion in Everglades restoration and water quality since taking office in January 2019 — a figure he said has never been matched in state history. He said his administration set an initial funding goal, beat it by nearly $1 billion in his first term, then set a second-term goal of $3.5 billion and has reached nearly $6 billion.The governor said his administration has completed or broken ground on more than 90 Everglades projects and has reached more project milestones than any previous administration in Florida history. He cited reductions of 5.6 million pounds of nitrogen per year and nearly 1 million pounds of phosphorus per year as among the tangible results of those investments.DeSantis also highlighted progress on the Everglades Agricultural Area reservoir south of Lake Okeechobee, which he said was originally scheduled for completion in 2034. Through a partnership with the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers announced after President Donald Trump took office in January 2025, the project is now projected to be completed by 2029 and at nearly half the original federal cost estimate."Isn't that something — what you want — under budget, ahead of schedule," DeSantis said.The EAA reservoir is designed to store 78 billion gallons of water and deliver 270 billion to 470 billion gallons of clean freshwater each year to the Everglades and Florida Bay.Bartlett said the pump station at the C-23 project site is capable of moving 166 million gallons of water every day — comparable in capacity to Miami's drinking water system — and has been operational since May 14."We haven't had a lost summer since you've been in office, Governor," Bartlett said. "Have not had a lost summer."Lambert pointed to measurable environmental improvements since DeSantis took office, including seagrass returning to stable levels in the Indian River Lagoon and Saint Lucie Estuary, supporting fish and manatee populations as well as the ecotourism industry. The Indian River Lagoon and Saint Lucie Estuary are home to more than 4,000 species of plant and wildlife.DeSantis said the broader Everglades restoration effort is the largest and most ambitious restoration project in U.S. history."When you think about America 250 — a massive country that spans a continent from sea to shining sea — there have been a lot of things that have been done over those 250 years, and there's never been a project of this magnitude that has been attempted, much less brought to fruition like we have," DeSantis said.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Postal Service from implementing Trump’s directive. The Postal Service has said it would not deliver ballots from states that did not pre-clear their envelope design with the federal government and submit a list of voters to an online portal, which has yet to be activated.Election officials warn that it’s impossible to comply with those terms, especially with the first mail ballots arleady being sent out in Alabama, North Carolina and Wisconsin.The panel of three judges nominated by former President Joe Biden agreed with the plaintiffs that the president does not have the power to regulate states’ election policy.RELATED STORY | Trump administration asks Supreme Court to allow mail-in voting limits before midterms“Appellants have not made a strong showing that the district court erred in determining that the Final Rule is likely unlawful,” they wrote, a reference to rule published by the Postal Service to implement Trump’s order.The panel’s decision comes even as the Supreme Court is already considering the same case, which is part of a frenzied legal rush as states are beginning to send out mail ballots for this fall’s midterm elections. By: Aja Dorsainvil Posted FORT PIERCE, Fla. — Fort Pierce police are investigating the death of an unidentified man who was found lying in the grass near a business on Okeechobee Road Wednesday morning. Officers said they responded to the 7000 block of Okeechobee Road shortly before 7 a.m. after receiving reports of an unresponsive man lying in the grass near a business. Lucie County Fire Rescue also responded to the incident and the man was pronounced dead at the scene. According to police, a witness told investigators they had seen the man lying in the same area the night before but believed he was sleeping. Detectives said they found no obvious signs of foul play and the Medical Examiner's Office will determine the cause and manner of death. Detectives said they are working to identify the man and the investigation remains active.

Students and staff at Martin County High School were evacuated Thursday afternoon after a bomb threat was received via email, according to school officials. In a message sent to families, school administrators said there was an increased law enforcement presence on campus as authorities responded to the threat. The Martin County Sheriff's Office is conducting a comprehensive search of the school property while students and staff remain evacuated away from campus buildings. School officials emphasized that all students and staff are safe as the investigation continues. "Please know that students and staff remain safe," the school said in its notification to families. "We will provide an update once there is new information to share." It remains unclear whether any suspicious items have been found or how long the search will take. Authorities have not released additional details about the source of the email threat. Parents were notified of the situation through a message from the school Thursday afternoon. No evidence of threat found In an update issued at 2:55 p.m., school officials said the Martin County Sheriff's Office was finalizing its sweep of the campus and found no evidence of a threat. Students and staff were cleared to return to their classrooms, and regular dismissal procedures were expected to continue as scheduled. School officials also said bus transportation was anticipated to operate without delays. "Thank you for your patience and cooperation as we worked with law enforcement to ensure the safety of our students and staff," the school said in its update. Authorities have not released additional details about the source of the email threat. This story will be updated if more information becomes available. Former President George W. Bush gave rare insight into his experience on Sept. came under attack by al-Qaida.Appearing with Condoleezza Rice, who served as his national security adviser, Bush spoke Wednesday from his presidential center two days before the 25th anniversary of the attacks.RELATED STORY | King Charles III and Queen Camilla honor 9/11 victims at Ground Zero in New YorkBush was at a Florida elementary school on the morning of the attacks. As the Twin Towers in New York City crumbled and civilian aircraft were grounded, Bush was whisked across the country aboard Air Force One instead of returning directly to Washington.Bush said that when he first learned an airplane had hit one of the Twin Towers, he assumed it was an accident. It was not until a second plane hit the other tower that he realized the magnitude of what was unfolding.“It was pretty clear to me that we were under attack,” Bush said. “My job was to defend the child that was reading to me and her family and her country.”“I became a wartime president,” Bush added. “There’s no doubt in my mind that this was not a law enforcement event. This was a war, and the job of the president and his team was to rally the nation to do what was necessary to protect our people.”Amid the chaos of closing U.S. airspace following the attacks in New York and at the Pentagon outside Washington, the White House believed the military had shot down Flight 93 over Shanksville, Pennsylvania.RELATED STORY | Five suspected 9/11 terrorists were never tried after the attacks“There was this horrible moment where the vice president kept trying to get confirmation as to what had happened,” Rice said. “And for about 10 minutes, we thought we’d shot down a civilian aircraft. That always represented to me just how hard the decisions were that you had to make under a lot of pressure.”It was one of several confusing incidents that occurred that day. Bush also said he was rushed to the White House bunker when a military aircraft was mistakenly identified as flying toward Andrews Air Force Base.Bush is expected to attend a remembrance ceremony Friday at the site of the Twin Towers in New York.

Every fall, at the start of the school year, a Port St. Lucie social studies teacher takes her students back to a day they never lived through.WATCH BELOW: 'They deserved to be remembered. Their legacy deserves to be carried on,' Ayleen Charles tells WPTV's Zitlali SolacheAyleen Charles has been teaching for over a decade. Each year, she makes Sept. 11 a centerpiece of her classroom."It's important to keep that memory alive, because that what history is right?" Ron DeSantis on Wednesday celebrated the completion of the C-23 Canal Estuary Discharge Diversion Project in Martin County, calling it part of the largest environmental restoration effort in U.S. The project, located at 10297 Southwest Martin Highway, will reroute excess water from the C-23 Canal away from the South Fork of the Saint Lucie River — where it had previously contributed to harmful algal blooms — and instead send it through a nearly 7-mile interconnect canal to the C-44 Reservoir and Stormwater Treatment Area. DeSantis was joined at the ribbon-cutting by Florida Department of Environmental Protection Secretary Alexis Lambert and South Florida Water Management District Executive Director Drew Bartlett, along with district board members Chairman Goss, Ronnie Bergeron, Ben Butler, Charlotte Roman, Tom Hurley and Robert Spotswood Jr. Since entering its operational testing phase in May, the project has diverted nearly 5 billion gallons of water away from the Saint Lucie Estuary. When operating at full capacity, the pump stations can fill an Olympic-size swimming pool in just under 6 minutes. Lambert said the project is projected to prevent 55,000 pounds of nitrogen and 14,000 pounds of phosphorus from entering the Saint Lucie River on average each year, and will divert 6.3 billion gallons of water from the river to the C-44 Reservoir and Stormwater Treatment Area. "Florida's waterways are a deeply interconnected system and preventing these harmful discharges will further improve the health of the estuary and the lagoon," Lambert said. DeSantis said his administration has invested close to $10 billion in Everglades restoration and water quality since taking office in January 2019 — a figure he said has never been matched in state history. He said his administration set an initial funding goal, beat it by nearly $1 billion in his first term, then set a second-term goal of $3.5 billion and has reached nearly $6 billion. The governor said his administration has completed or broken ground on more than 90 Everglades projects and has reached more project milestones than any previous administration in Florida history. He cited reductions of 5.6 million pounds of nitrogen per year and nearly 1 million pounds of phosphorus per year as among the tangible results of those investments. DeSantis also highlighted progress on the Everglades Agricultural Area reservoir south of Lake Okeechobee, which he said was originally scheduled for completion in 2034. Through a partnership with the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers announced after President Donald Trump took office in January 2025, the project is now projected to be completed by 2029 and at nearly half the original federal cost estimate. "Isn't that something — what you want — under budget, ahead of schedule," DeSantis said. The EAA reservoir is designed to store 78 billion gallons of water and deliver 270 billion to 470 billion gallons of clean freshwater each year to the Everglades and Florida Bay. Bartlett said the pump station at the C-23 project site is capable of moving 166 million gallons of water every day — comparable in capacity to Miami's drinking water system — and has been operational since May 14. "We haven't had a lost summer since you've been in office, Governor," Bartlett said. "Have not had a lost summer." Lambert pointed to measurable environmental improvements since DeSantis took office, including seagrass returning to stable levels in the Indian River Lagoon and Saint Lucie Estuary, supporting fish and manatee populations as well as the ecotourism industry. The Indian River Lagoon and Saint Lucie Estuary are home to more than 4,000 species of plant and wildlife. DeSantis said the broader Everglades restoration effort is the largest and most ambitious restoration project in U.S. "When you think about America 250 — a massive country that spans a continent from sea to shining sea — there have been a lot of things that have been done over those 250 years, and there's never been a project of this magnitude that has been attempted, much less brought to fruition like we have," DeSantis said. A nearly 85-acre entertainment district is in the works in Port St. Lucie along Village Parkway in the Tradition community, and developers say new restaurants and stores could arrive sooner than expected. Gustavo Lumer, CEO of Lumer Real Estate, is behind the property that would become the Tradition Entertainment District. The development is divided between four parcels along Village Parkway from Innovation Way to Hegener Drive. Lumer said he hopes to bring in around 25 new restaurants and additional stores to the area. “There’s a need for diversity, and they keep telling us that they want different options,” Lumer said. Development will start on a 5.5-acre parcel off Innovation Way, which will include 40,000 square feet of retail and restaurant space. Lumer said 60 percent of that space is already leased, and he expects construction to start within six months. “The retailers are eager to open yesterday. If we could pop it up next week and have it there, they’re ready to go,” Lumer said. The next phase will develop 2 parcels totaling around 60 acres farther south, near the new Stars and Stripes Park. Lumer said this section would be the “hub” of the entertainment district. Plans include potentially 15 restaurants, a luxury gym, grocery stores, retail and possibly a movie theater. “It’ll be a place where you can park or come with your golf cart and spend the afternoon going around different places,” Lumer said. Lumer said the district will help keep and attract business in Port St. “The more brands that they keep opening, everybody’s realizing, well, I’m the only one missing out, and so you’ll see a lot of beautiful brands coming in a short, short time,” Lumer said. Neighbors in the area said they welcome the development. LaVaughn Harvey said he would visit often. “I’d be there a lot more,” Harvey said. Neighbor Tina Gramata said the district fills a community need. “We need more places for people to go on a regular basis to intermingle,” Gramata said. Lumer said they are still working on final site approvals for the first parcel off Innovation Way and will begin working on site plan approval for the remaining three sites. “That’s a lot of retail and a lot of restaurants, and hopefully we can bring entertainment venues,” Lumer said.

Indian River County deputies arrested two men in separate cases involving alleged illegal saw palmetto berry harvesting over the Labor Day weekend, according to arrest affidavits. Corey Michael Smith, of Vero Beach, was arrested Sept. 4 after deputies responded to a trespassing call at a BP gas station on 9th Street Southwest, the affidavit states. A deputy said a helicopter crew had spotted Smith on Indian River County School Board property near 800 20th Ave. Deputies found him at the gas station with five black bags containing saw palmetto stalks, according to the affidavit. Smith allegedly showed deputies a palmetto berry harvesting permit that listed an address on 17th Avenue Southwest. The affidavit says the property owner told deputies Smith did not have permission to harvest on the property, which belongs to the Salvation Army . Smith was arrested on charges of using a false or forged palmetto berry harvest permit, disclosing police radio information to aid a suspect, and trespassing after a warning. The affidavit states a deputy heard dispatch traffic coming from a scanner app on Smith’s phone while he was detained. A day later, deputies arrested Francis Ostrowski after a sheriff’s office camera in the North County Conservation Area near 7800 130th St. captured a man carrying a bag filled with saw palmetto berries, according to his affidavit. See also: South Florida crypto kingpin pleads guilty in alleged $245M theft conspiracy Deputies located Ostrowski nearby with a bag of berries and asked whether he had a permit to harvest them. Ostrowski said he did not, the affidavit states. Ostrowski was arrested on a felony charge of harvesting an endangered plant without a permit. The arrests come amid a series of recent saw palmetto berry cases across the Treasure Coast. CBS12 previously reported on arrests involving the alleged theft of about 200 pounds of berries in Martin County and about 150 pounds in Indian River County . In another recent case, a Boynton Beach man was arrested after deputies said they found about 500 pounds of saw palmetto berries .

Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier was in West Palm Beach Thursday morning to announce the arrests of two alleged ringleaders in a coordinated baby formula theft operation that spanned multiple counties and resulted in over $1 million in stolen merchandise.Mohammed Alsaidi and Zeina Zabib, both of Lake Worth, were arrested on charges of conspiracy to commit racketeering and directing and dealing in stolen property. If convicted, they each face up to 90 years in prison.WATCH THE FULL PRESS CONFERENCE BELOW:The 15-month investigation, dubbed "Formula One," uncovered what authorities describe as a sophisticated criminal enterprise involving nearly a dozen individuals across six judicial circuits. The operation included more than 150 separate baby formula thefts from major retailers including Publix, Walmart, Target, Walgreens and CVS."This wasn't just a little bit of retail theft here or there," Uthmeier said. "This was a large, coordinated enterprise spanning over multiple counties and many circuits."Detective Christopher Apple of the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office led the investigation. Apple explained that professional shoplifters, known as "boosters," stole baby formula and sold it to Alsaidi and Zabib, who acted as "fences" — purchasing the stolen goods and reselling them for profit at about five times what they paid.When authorities executed search warrants on Sept. 1, they found about 1,000 cans of baby formula worth about $38,000 in retail value in a warehouse in Davie that was not air-conditioned, along with 1,300 cans of tuna and sardines stored in temperatures exceeding 90 degrees.Nine other individuals have already been arrested in connection with the scheme, Uthmeier said.The arrests come as Florida has strengthened penalties for retail theft. Ron DeSantis signed HB 549, which allows repeat retail theft cases to be prosecuted as first-degree felonies carrying up to 30 years in prison.Uthmeier emphasized that retail theft is not a victimless crime, pointing to empty store shelves, increased security costs and higher prices for consumers as consequences of such operations."You don't want to upset moms ever. You certainly don't want to upset moms when it comes to feeding their little ones," Uthmeier said. "So, this is a fight that we will valiantly fight."

A former Fort Pierce police officer was arrested after investigators say he accessed Flock and other databases hundreds of times to track his ex-girlfriend. Josepher Crutchfield, who resigned from the Fort Pierce Police Department last month, was arrested Tuesday on four felony counts related to unauthorized computer access, according to the department. He was being held at the St. Lucie County Jail on $80,000 secured bond. Flock cameras are license plate readers law enforcement can use to help identify vehicles connected to suspects in crimes. "The cameras are here for our community's safety, not to be abused by those who are entrusted to safeguarding," said Fort Pierce Police Chief David Smith. Crutchfield had previously faced an Internal Affairs investigation over allegations of sexually inappropriate behavior toward female Fort Pierce police employees in 2021. Investigators said his behavior was excessive, unwelcome, and affected the employees' work environment. The department ultimately found he violated five policies and suspended him for two days without pay. The latest investigation began on Aug. 10, 2026 after the department was contacted by the media about concerns over possible misuse of its Flock automated license plate reader system. Crutchfield was placed on administrative leave on Aug. 7, 2026 and his access to law enforcement systems was revoked. A criminal investigation began Aug. Crutchfield resigned days later on Aug. 18 before the investigation was completed. Investigators later determined there was probable cause for his arrest. Chief Smith called the incident a black eye for the department. "The public places immense trust in those who wear this badge, and with that trust comes a tremendous responsibility. No one is above the law," he said. See also: Details of a Fort Pierce police officer's harassment that got him suspended without pay Between October 2025 and July 2026, Crutchfield allegedly accessed the Flock database 382 times to search the same license plate, using different reason categories and without a legitimate law enforcement purpose. Most of the searches were made while he was off duty. Investigators determined the vehicle was registered to an ex-girlfriend. The investigation expanded to other databases, including FCIC , NCIC , DAVID and TLO . Investigators found Crutchfield made additional searches over the last few years to look up people's names and personal information - searches that they said had no legitimate law enforcement purpose. Those databases contain restricted personal information, including addresses and dates of birth. Officers must acknowledge a warning each time they access the systems, confirming they are being used for legitimate law enforcement purposes. The chief said investigators are not speculating about Crutchfield's intentions or whether the alleged conduct amounted to stalking, but they will follow any additional leads. "The conduct alleged in this case is unacceptable and represents a serious breach of the trust that's placed in law enforcement," Smith said. " Again, it does not diminish the dedicated work that our officers do every day." The department has launched a broader audit of its law enforcement databases. So far, officials said no additional violations have been identified. Fort Pierce police have also tightened access to the Flock system. Only lieutenants and higher ranking officers can now use it, and each search requires approval from one of two deputy chiefs and a case number. Flock searches will be limited to forcible felony investigations and missing or endangered person cases. The department also cut its data retention period from 30 days to seven days. "The system will not be used for general investigative surveillance, intelligence gathering unrelated to an authorized investigation, or routine investigative inquiries," said Smith. Officials also added a position within the Office of Professional Standards to conduct monthly audits of law enforcement databases. The chief acknowledged the incident is a setback for the department but said officials are committed to being transparent and holding officers accountable. "This is a black eye for the agency," the chief said. "This is a difficult moment for our organization and our community, but our responsibility is clear. The authority entrusted to police officers comes with an extraordinary responsibility. When there is criminal evidence that an officer may have violated the law, we have an obligation to act. The badge does not provide immunity from accountability."

This week, I found myself somewhere that smells absolutely incredible and where creativity meets deliciousness. But wait – I had some unexpected company! I spotted our very own Ashley Glass there!Angela, one of the talented folks at Jupiter Donuts, was ready to teach us some fun doughnut making abilities. Before I went behind the counter, I learned that the bakers start working at around midnight, with decorators arriving by 3 a.m. to hand-cut, make, and decorate over 40 varieties of scratch-made goodies.The technique was all about the swirl with a little flick of the wrist, Angela explained as she demonstrated. I tried my best with that little swirl, and Ashley had a really good flip that I liked.Of course, I had to put my own meteorologist twist on it. I created a rainbow-themed donut, because what better way to represent the weather than with a colorful rainbow?I was getting excited about my own creation and asked Angela how I did with the dip because I thought it looked awesome. Angela gave me some honest feedback – she thought I did phenomenal, but she had to admit she was loving Ashley's creation a little bit more. She did say I had the frosting down the sides with perfect ratio. Angela was impressed with how it came out and asked if I'd love a job with them. I immediately said yes – I mean, who wouldn't want to work with donuts all day?What struck me most about this experience wasn't just how delicious everything looked – it was the artistry and creativity that goes into each and every doughnut at Jupiter Donuts. From Ashley's beach scenes to sunshine designs to my meteorologist-inspired cumulonimbus cloud, these aren't just treats – they're edible works of art!

A former Fort Pierce police officer accused of misusing law enforcement databases to track his ex-girlfriend is expected to make his first court appearance Wednesday. Police say Josepher Crutchfield searched his ex-girlfriend’s vehicle in the department’s Flock license plate reader system 382 times between October 2025 and July 2026 without a legitimate law enforcement reason. Investigators say Crutchfield also used other police databases to search for personal information. He was placed on administrative leave in August and later resigned from the department. Crutchfield now faces four felony charges related to unauthorized computer access. He was being held at the St. Lucie County Jail on $80,000 secured bond. Fort Pierce police have since tightened access to the Flock system and started a broader audit of department databases. Now, the chief says a departmentwide audit is underway, and so far, no other violations have been found. CBS12 News will be following Crutchfield’s first appearance and will bring you updates from court. This is a developing story.

Every fall, at the start of the school year, a Port St. Lucie social studies teacher takes her students back to a day they never lived through.WATCH BELOW: 'They deserved to be remembered. Their legacy deserves to be carried on,' Ayleen Charles tells WPTV's Zitlali SolacheAyleen Charles has been teaching at Sunlight Christian Academy for nearly a decade. Each year, she makes Sept. 11 a centerpiece of her classroom."It's important to keep that memory alive, because that what history is right?" Charles said.Charles said her students have only ever known a world shaped by the attacks."You were born in a world shaped by 9/11. They don't know what it's like to be in a world that was not shaped by 9/11," Charles said.To make the history feel real, she uses survivor stories, images and audio recordings — including firsthand accounts from those who were there."I let them read first hand accounts of voicemails that were left from people on the airplane. I make it very real for them," Charles said.Part of that reality includes explaining how everyday life changed after the attacks — including at airports."They're shocked when I tell them we used to be able to go to the airport, pass what would be TSA now, and actually see the airplanes take off," Charles said.But Charles said the lessons go beyond security changes and emergency preparedness."But it also shows us the choices that were made after — how we came together as a nation," Charles said.As the years pass, she said the responsibility to remember will be carried forward by the students she teaches."I want students to remember the realness of what I taught them. I want them to remember that this is not just something printed in a history book," Charles said. "I want to them to remember how that impacted the people that they know and the world that they currently live in today."For Charles, the mission is personal — and urgent."People deserved to be remembered. The people that lost their lives, because of an act of hatred," she said. "They deserved to be remembered. Their legacy deserves to be carried on."To hear more stories be sure to watch Echoes of September: A 9/11 Special on Friday, Sept. on WPTVThis story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Boca Raton's new police chief says building a new headquarters is his top priority — and he wants to put the question back to voters.Chief Jarad Phelps, who has been on the job for a few weeks, said told WPTV Boca Raton reporter Victor Jorges that he is focused on moving the project forward after voters earlier this year rejected a ballot measure to fund a new facility.WATCH BELOW: Boca's new police chief makes new headquarters top priority"Right now my No. 1 priority is the police station. The conversations we've been having about a new police station, and getting it to voters on whether or not they want to bond to fund that," Phelps said.The issue is expected to return to voters at the next municipal election. The city has presented two options for a potential new headquarters.One option is a 16-acre campus at Spanish River, featuring a main building and a downtown substation. The second option would keep the facility downtown in a 6-story building. City staff says the downtown plan could cost about 10% more due to vertical construction.Phelps described the current building's condition as alarming, warning it could put evidence at risk."This is a deteriorating building. I'm not going to point fingers in the past; I'm trying to move forward, but the condition of this building is lacking in a lot of different areas. You get a rainstorm, the roof leaks consistently," Phelps said.Phelps also said the city's police department is "spread out" throughout the city, and a new headquarters could centralize the team. For more updates related to Boca Raton, follow along on our Let's Hear It Facebook Page.

President Donald Trump said he would give American adults $5,000 each to spend in the United States if Republicans win November’s midterm elections. Trump made the remarks Wednesday while campaigning for Republicans at a midterm convention in Dallas.Trump has made similar promises before, including proposals to reimburse Americans for tariff costs and DOGE-related cuts, though neither has materialized. He said Republicans would need to win both the House and Senate for the payments to be issued.With over 260 million U.S. adults, the cost of such a proposal would be over $1 trillion.RELATED STORY | Are taxpayers getting a refund check from DOGE? Musk says he'll check with TrumpPolls currently suggest Democrats could regain control of at least one chamber of Congress. Historically, the party out of power in the White House often gains seats during midterm elections.Trump is making himself a central figure in the campaign, hoping voters will continue backing his agenda and Republican candidates aligned with him.“Because of our tremendous strength and success economically, I will issue a dividend to every adult citizen in the United States of America for $5,000,” Trump said. “The only caveat I have is that the dividend ... must be spent in the United States of America.”Trump said he did not want the money spent in other countries, specifically mentioning China, Germany and Canada.“If the Republicans win, you win with us and you get $5,000,” Trump said.RELATED STORY | Trump says Americans will get payments of 'at least $2,000' from tariff revenueHow likely is a Republican win?According to the Cook Political Report, control of Congress could hinge on 21 toss-up House races and six toss-up Senate races. Assuming each party wins the seats that currently lean in its favor, Republicans would need to win nine of the 21 House toss-ups and three of the six Senate toss-ups.

After months of delays, public pushback and political debate, West Palm Beach's controversial Downtown Master Plan update is moving forward again — but not without major changes and lingering concerns from residents.During a nearly four-hour Downtown Action Committee meeting, city officials, planners, engineers, residents and neighborhood advocates packed the room — a sharp contrast from earlier discussions.WATCH BELOW: West Palm Beach removes waterfront high-rises from master plan"Those meetings were like ghost towns," said Mike Schmidt, vice president of the Downtown Neighborhood Association. "Now it's like a Taylor Swift press conference."City officials say the Downtown Master Plan update is needed because West Palm Beach is growing rapidly and evolving into a nationally recognized urban center. Leaders say they want to better connect CityPlace and downtown, encourage housing options and guide development in a way that improves quality of life.But residents argue growth is already straining infrastructure and changing the character of the city too quickly."We do not experience development one project at a time — it's all together," Fatima Sanandaji, co-founder of Save West Palm Beach said.Officials presented data showing downtown growth has actually slowed compared to previous years. Between 2015 and 2025, the city averaged roughly 290 new residential units per year downtown.Still, downtown now contains more than 9,000 residential units, and residents repeatedly questioned whether roads, emergency services and parking can keep up.Traffic dominated much of the discussion.City traffic engineer Saurabh Basnet said some intersections are nearing capacity, especially Okeechobee Boulevard."It's at about 98% capacity," Basnet told the committee.Officials said future improvements could help relieve congestion, including:New road connections such as Fern StreetAdaptive traffic signals that respond to real-time traffic conditionsExpanded Palm Tran serviceSafer walking and biking infrastructureTransportation demand management strategies aimed at reducing vehicle tripsBasnet said if the city does nothing, congestion could significantly worsen by 2045.But many residents said the city's traffic analysis does not reflect reality.“We are being told traffic is manageable. That is simply not the lived experience of residents," said India Foster with the West Palm Beach Residents Coalition.Others questioned whether studies account for seasonal residents, construction impacts and future development already in the pipeline.Concerns also came from the West Palm Beach firefighters union, which said taller buildings create unique emergency response challenges. Such as longer wait times due to firefighters needing to climb more stories.Ryan Stacey, speaking on behalf of the firefighters union, said the department is "aggressively neutral" on growth but disappointed the plan does not specifically address first responder needs."If it's on a 25-story building, very different than a short building," he said.He noted the department has added 84 firefighters and a new truck in recent years but said future planning must include police and fire staffing needs as downtown density increases."I think a continued pause is absolutely warranted," he said.The most significant revision to the plan involves the Flagler Waterfront District.An earlier proposal would have allowed buildings up to 25 stories along portions of the waterfront through development incentives. That proposal has now been removed.Under the updated version:Most of Flagler Drive will remain capped at five storiesAreas north of Banyan Boulevard can still allow up to eight stories under existing incentivesTaller development would instead be concentrated farther inland in designated downtown districtsResidents who opposed high-rise waterfront development celebrated the change."This is an important step," said Schmidt agreed."What's going on here is showing some of our comments are bearing fruit," he said.Still, some warned that taller buildings just one block west of Flagler could still impact waterfront views and infrastructure.City documents presented to neighborhood groups outlined several additional revisions:Downtown parks along Flagler Drive remain protected as Urban Open SpaceNew large developments must reduce projected vehicle trips by 25%Nonresidential parking requirements south of Banyan Boulevard would be reduced by 20%Residential parking requirements would remain unchangedProjects using development incentives would face stronger workforce housing requirementsWorkforce housing affordability periods would increase from 20 years to 30 yearsDevelopers using city incentives would need to provide more affordable housing or pay city feesA major point of tension emerged over timing.A separate mayor-appointed Neighborhood Partnership Network has spent the last two months researching downtown growth and says it still has hundreds of unanswered questions.Members told the committee they were surprised the process was moving ahead before their recommendations were complete."If there's a group the mayor put together and they are saying wait — what's happening?" asked Downtown Action Committee board member Michael Bakst.Jessica Swift, a member of the partnership group, said volunteers have spent 65 days researching the issue and still need more time."We are volunteers," Swift said. "We have no intention to hold up this process."She said the group has submitted 180 questions to the city and received answers to only seven.Others argued the city is moving too quickly on decisions that could permanently reshape West Palm Beach."Once adopted, West Palm Beach will be changed forever and difficult to reverse," Sanandaji warned.DAC board members emphasized the Downtown Action Committee only serves in an advisory role.The final decisions will be made by the West Palm Beach City Commission.Officials also clarified that if no updates are approved, some existing development incentives from prior plans could still allow high-rise projects along portions of Flagler Drive under current regulations.After lengthy debate, the committee voted to move the recommendations forward.The first reading before city commissioners is expected on Oct. 26, with a final vote anticipated next year.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. A Palm Beach County woman received a surprise welcome home after Habitat for Humanity of Greater Palm Beach County and the iTHINK Community Foundation transformed her new house into a fully furnished home.Carla Hamilton officially received the keys to her new home this week after completing hundreds of volunteer hours through Habitat for Humanity's homeownership program."This is a home that she worked very hard for," said Jennifer Thomason, president and CEO of Habitat for Humanity of Greater Palm Beach County. "She volunteered 300 to 400 hours building her home, doing financial education, and then she purchased her home at a 0% interest mortgage based on 30% of her income and not the market."Hamilton and her grandson walked into the home expecting an empty house but instead found every room completely furnished and personalized."We were surprised," Hamilton said. I noticed it was full of furniture. The stuff wasn't here the last time she visited. It was just an empty box, and now there's things like coffee makers and juicers and TVs and every drawer, every cabinet has something in it."The home makeover was coordinated by the iTHINK Community Foundation and dozens of volunteers who worked behind the scenes to prepare the surprise reveal.Stephen Johnson, AVP of administration and marketing for iTHINK Financial, said the organization partnered with Habitat for Humanity as part of the foundation’s ongoing community investment efforts."Our iTHINK Community Foundation is how we made this happen,” Johnson said. "We're celebrating 10 years of doing things like this in our communities. We've invested over a million dollars doing programs with Habitat for Humanity and other really good organizations here in Palm Beach County.”Organizers said volunteers used information from a questionnaire completed by Hamilton to personalize the home with meaningful details connected to her family and interests."That was on my list," Hamilton said while reacting to items throughout the house. "That was my favorite song (American Authors 'Best Day of My Life' There [the lyrics are] on the wall."Larissa, one of the iTHINK volunteer organizers, said volunteers transformed the house in just a few hours."We had 31 volunteers on last Saturday morning — kids, families, brothers, uncles, you name them, they were all here," she said. "We came into the house just over three hours, furnished it, staged it. It was really fun."Affordable housing remains a major challenge for many South Florida families as home prices continue rising across Palm Beach County. Habitat for Humanity programs help qualifying families achieve homeownership through sweat equity, financial education and affordable mortgage opportunities.Habitat for Humanity of Greater Palm Beach County partners with local organizations and volunteers to build homes and support long-term housing stability throughout the region.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI.
