The trial for Palm City dog trainer and boarder Nikki Camerlengo has been delayed until 2027 — at least the ninth continuance in a case that began more than two years ago.In court Wednesday morning, prosecutor Kristin Chase said one of the state's key witnesses is on medical disability and told Judge Elizabeth Metzger that doctors say she cannot testify until at least the end of January.That witness must first testify at a hearing to determine whether she will be allowed to take the stand at trial. Metzger is now aiming for February for that hearing, pushing any potential trial date even further back.Camerlengo faces two counts of animal cruelty in the deaths of two dogs, deputies say, that died while in the care of her Palm City training and boarding facility, Pawsitively Paradise. She was arrested in 2024 after Martin County detectives said the dogs died in her care. A WPTV investigation linked at least seven dog deaths or serious injuries to Pawsitively Paradise over the course of a decade.Her attorneys are now asking the judge to throw out the case altogether. Court records show the defense, on Sept. 2, filed a motion to dismiss, and Metzger ordered both sides to set a hearing on that motion by the end of this week.Camerlengo's next court date is set for December, though the judge could take up the motion to dismiss sooner.The latest delay comes after a contentious July 2026 hearing in which Metzger pressed both the prosecution and defense over why the case still hadn't gone to trial."I wanted you here, because I thought I was very clear in the past on what you needed to do," Metzger said at that hearing. "This case has been continued so many times, I've lost count."At one point, an exchange between Metzger and Camerlengo's defense attorney, Stuart Kaplan, grew heated."Your Honor, it's of no fault of the defendant," Kaplan said."I'm not saying that," Metzger said."You're looking at me!" Kaplan said."I'm not saying that!" Metzger replied.Kaplan has asked the court to block testimony from both the Texas veterinary pathologist who performed the two necropsies and from lead investigator Detective Christine Polizzi."I think the detective jumped the gun, so to speak. I don't think she had all of the facts," Kaplan told WPTV.The hearing to decide whether those witnesses can testify has not yet taken place.For Adele Kirk Csontos, the wait for justice started even before Camerlengo's arrest. She filed a police report after her dog, Mako, died following 48 hours at Pawsitively Paradise in November 2022."I was devastated. It's probably going to sound crazy, but I literally for two weeks I couldn't talk to my friends," Kirk Csontos said. "I felt responsible."Camerlengo was never charged in Mako's death — his necropsy was inconclusive. Necropsies of two other dogs concluded they died from blunt force trauma, leading to her arrest and charges."I mean, I know the wheels of justice turn very slowly, but no, I didn't think it would be two years," Kirk Csontos said.Despite the ongoing delays, Kirk Csontos said she has not given up hope."I'm still hopeful. Believe it or not, I'm still hopeful that she will be held accountable," Kirk Csontos said.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Ron DeSantis on Wednesday celebrated the completion of the C-23 Canal Estuary Discharge Diversion Project in Martin County, calling it part of the largest environmental restoration effort in U.S. The project, located at 10297 Southwest Martin Highway, will reroute excess water from the C-23 Canal away from the South Fork of the Saint Lucie River — where it had previously contributed to harmful algal blooms — and instead send it through a nearly 7-mile interconnect canal to the C-44 Reservoir and Stormwater Treatment Area. DeSantis was joined at the ribbon-cutting by Florida Department of Environmental Protection Secretary Alexis Lambert and South Florida Water Management District Executive Director Drew Bartlett, along with district board members Chairman Goss, Ronnie Bergeron, Ben Butler, Charlotte Roman, Tom Hurley and Robert Spotswood Jr. Since entering its operational testing phase in May, the project has diverted nearly 5 billion gallons of water away from the Saint Lucie Estuary. When operating at full capacity, the pump stations can fill an Olympic-size swimming pool in just under 6 minutes. Lambert said the project is projected to prevent 55,000 pounds of nitrogen and 14,000 pounds of phosphorus from entering the Saint Lucie River on average each year, and will divert 6.3 billion gallons of water from the river to the C-44 Reservoir and Stormwater Treatment Area. "Florida's waterways are a deeply interconnected system and preventing these harmful discharges will further improve the health of the estuary and the lagoon," Lambert said. DeSantis said his administration has invested close to $10 billion in Everglades restoration and water quality since taking office in January 2019 — a figure he said has never been matched in state history. He said his administration set an initial funding goal, beat it by nearly $1 billion in his first term, then set a second-term goal of $3.5 billion and has reached nearly $6 billion. The governor said his administration has completed or broken ground on more than 90 Everglades projects and has reached more project milestones than any previous administration in Florida history. He cited reductions of 5.6 million pounds of nitrogen per year and nearly 1 million pounds of phosphorus per year as among the tangible results of those investments. DeSantis also highlighted progress on the Everglades Agricultural Area reservoir south of Lake Okeechobee, which he said was originally scheduled for completion in 2034. Through a partnership with the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers announced after President Donald Trump took office in January 2025, the project is now projected to be completed by 2029 and at nearly half the original federal cost estimate. "Isn't that something — what you want — under budget, ahead of schedule," DeSantis said. The EAA reservoir is designed to store 78 billion gallons of water and deliver 270 billion to 470 billion gallons of clean freshwater each year to the Everglades and Florida Bay. Bartlett said the pump station at the C-23 project site is capable of moving 166 million gallons of water every day — comparable in capacity to Miami's drinking water system — and has been operational since May 14. "We haven't had a lost summer since you've been in office, Governor," Bartlett said. "Have not had a lost summer." Lambert pointed to measurable environmental improvements since DeSantis took office, including seagrass returning to stable levels in the Indian River Lagoon and Saint Lucie Estuary, supporting fish and manatee populations as well as the ecotourism industry. The Indian River Lagoon and Saint Lucie Estuary are home to more than 4,000 species of plant and wildlife. DeSantis said the broader Everglades restoration effort is the largest and most ambitious restoration project in U.S. "When you think about America 250 — a massive country that spans a continent from sea to shining sea — there have been a lot of things that have been done over those 250 years, and there's never been a project of this magnitude that has been attempted, much less brought to fruition like we have," DeSantis said. Ron DeSantis on Wednesday celebrated the completion of the C-23 Canal Estuary Discharge Diversion Project in Martin County, calling it part of the largest environmental restoration effort in U.S. The project, located at 10297 Southwest Martin Highway, will reroute excess water from the C-23 Canal away from the South Fork of the Saint Lucie River — where it had previously contributed to harmful algal blooms — and instead send it through a nearly 7-mile interconnect canal to the C-44 Reservoir and Stormwater Treatment Area. DeSantis was joined at the ribbon-cutting by Florida Department of Environmental Protection Secretary Alexis Lambert and South Florida Water Management District Executive Director Drew Bartlett, along with district board members Chairman Goss, Ronnie Bergeron, Ben Butler, Charlotte Roman, Tom Hurley and Robert Spotswood Jr. Since entering its operational testing phase in May, the project has diverted nearly 5 billion gallons of water away from the Saint Lucie Estuary. When operating at full capacity, the pump stations can fill an Olympic-size swimming pool in just under 6 minutes. Lambert said the project is projected to prevent 55,000 pounds of nitrogen and 14,000 pounds of phosphorus from entering the Saint Lucie River on average each year, and will divert 6.3 billion gallons of water from the river to the C-44 Reservoir and Stormwater Treatment Area. "Florida's waterways are a deeply interconnected system and preventing these harmful discharges will further improve the health of the estuary and the lagoon," Lambert said. DeSantis said his administration has invested close to $10 billion in Everglades restoration and water quality since taking office in January 2019 — a figure he said has never been matched in state history. He said his administration set an initial funding goal, beat it by nearly $1 billion in his first term, then set a second-term goal of $3.5 billion and has reached nearly $6 billion. The governor said his administration has completed or broken ground on more than 90 Everglades projects and has reached more project milestones than any previous administration in Florida history. He cited reductions of 5.6 million pounds of nitrogen per year and nearly 1 million pounds of phosphorus per year as among the tangible results of those investments. DeSantis also highlighted progress on the Everglades Agricultural Area reservoir south of Lake Okeechobee, which he said was originally scheduled for completion in 2034. Through a partnership with the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers announced after President Donald Trump took office in January 2025, the project is now projected to be completed by 2029 and at nearly half the original federal cost estimate. "Isn't that something — what you want — under budget, ahead of schedule," DeSantis said. The EAA reservoir is designed to store 78 billion gallons of water and deliver 270 billion to 470 billion gallons of clean freshwater each year to the Everglades and Florida Bay. Bartlett said the pump station at the C-23 project site is capable of moving 166 million gallons of water every day — comparable in capacity to Miami's drinking water system — and has been operational since May 14. "We haven't had a lost summer since you've been in office, Governor," Bartlett said. "Have not had a lost summer." Lambert pointed to measurable environmental improvements since DeSantis took office, including seagrass returning to stable levels in the Indian River Lagoon and Saint Lucie Estuary, supporting fish and manatee populations as well as the ecotourism industry. The Indian River Lagoon and Saint Lucie Estuary are home to more than 4,000 species of plant and wildlife. DeSantis said the broader Everglades restoration effort is the largest and most ambitious restoration project in U.S. "When you think about America 250 — a massive country that spans a continent from sea to shining sea — there have been a lot of things that have been done over those 250 years, and there's never been a project of this magnitude that has been attempted, much less brought to fruition like we have," DeSantis said. A former Fort Pierce police officer was arrested after investigators say he accessed Flock and other databases hundreds of times to track his ex-girlfriend. Josepher Crutchfield, who resigned from the Fort Pierce Police Department last month, was arrested Tuesday on four felony counts related to unauthorized computer access, according to the department. He was being held at the St. Lucie County Jail on $80,000 secured bond. Flock cameras are license plate readers law enforcement can use to help identify vehicles connected to suspects in crimes. "The cameras are here for our community's safety, not to be abused by those who are entrusted to safeguarding," said Fort Pierce Police Chief David Smith. Crutchfield had previously faced an Internal Affairs investigation over allegations of sexually inappropriate behavior toward female Fort Pierce police employees in 2021. Investigators said his behavior was excessive, unwelcome, and affected the employees' work environment. The department ultimately found he violated five policies and suspended him for two days without pay. The latest investigation began on Aug. 10, 2026 after the department was contacted by the media about concerns over possible misuse of its Flock automated license plate reader system. Crutchfield was placed on administrative leave on Aug. 7, 2026 and his access to law enforcement systems was revoked. A criminal investigation began Aug. Crutchfield resigned days later on Aug. 18 before the investigation was completed. Investigators later determined there was probable cause for his arrest. Chief Smith called the incident a black eye for the department. "The public places immense trust in those who wear this badge, and with that trust comes a tremendous responsibility. No one is above the law," he said. See also: Details of a Fort Pierce police officer's harassment that got him suspended without pay Between October 2025 and July 2026, Crutchfield allegedly accessed the Flock database 382 times to search the same license plate, using different reason categories and without a legitimate law enforcement purpose. Most of the searches were made while he was off duty. Investigators determined the vehicle was registered to an ex-girlfriend. The investigation expanded to other databases, including FCIC , NCIC , DAVID and TLO . Investigators found Crutchfield made additional searches over the last few years to look up people's names and personal information - searches that they said had no legitimate law enforcement purpose. Those databases contain restricted personal information, including addresses and dates of birth. Officers must acknowledge a warning each time they access the systems, confirming they are being used for legitimate law enforcement purposes. The chief said investigators are not speculating about Crutchfield's intentions or whether the alleged conduct amounted to stalking, but they will follow any additional leads. "The conduct alleged in this case is unacceptable and represents a serious breach of the trust that's placed in law enforcement," Smith said. " Again, it does not diminish the dedicated work that our officers do every day." The department has launched a broader audit of its law enforcement databases. So far, officials said no additional violations have been identified. Fort Pierce police have also tightened access to the Flock system. Only lieutenants and higher ranking officers can now use it, and each search requires approval from one of two deputy chiefs and a case number. Flock searches will be limited to forcible felony investigations and missing or endangered person cases. The department also cut its data retention period from 30 days to seven days. "The system will not be used for general investigative surveillance, intelligence gathering unrelated to an authorized investigation, or routine investigative inquiries," said Smith. Officials also added a position within the Office of Professional Standards to conduct monthly audits of law enforcement databases. The chief acknowledged the incident is a setback for the department but said officials are committed to being transparent and holding officers accountable. "This is a black eye for the agency," the chief said. "This is a difficult moment for our organization and our community, but our responsibility is clear. The authority entrusted to police officers comes with an extraordinary responsibility. When there is criminal evidence that an officer may have violated the law, we have an obligation to act. The badge does not provide immunity from accountability."

Palm Beach County is considering changes to its pet ordinance that would tighten rules for pet owners and hobby breeders — sparking debate over accountability and constitutional rights.The proposed ordinance would shorten the window for owners to reclaim lost pets from four business days to three. Owners of dangerous dogs would be required to carry a $100,000 liability insurance policy. Annual fees for hobby breeders would increase from $150 to $400, and yearly inspections would become mandatory.Local rescue groups, residents, and their dogs turned out to a meeting at the Vista Center to weigh in on the proposed changes.WATCH: Palm Beach County ordinance would raise breeder fees, require inspections for hobby breedersRebecca Landerman, executive director of Rescue Dog Network, said the ordinance is urgently needed. "We are growing in an ocean. And this ordinance is a lifejacket right now,” said Landerman.Rescue groups are pushing for stricter oversight, warning that irresponsible breeders can cause serious, lifelong health and behavior problems for dogs."We are such a crisis that we need laws to strengthen accountability to hold everyone responsible, when they do things that they shouldn't be doing," said Melody Aktinson with South Florida Mutt Rescue. Stacey Chiari Paladino, a dog rescuer and owner of Life with Reef, pointed to a recent case in a neighboring county as evidence that stronger rules are needed."We just saw what happened in Martin County where 36 border collies were removed from a breeder property from years and years of complaints," she said. "That should be a wakeup call."Chiari Paladino added that she would welcome inspections in the interest of animal welfare. "To save a dog from torture, I would allow anyone to rifle through my underwear drawer," she said. But some hobby breeders have raised concerns that mandatory inspections could violate Fourth Amendment protections against unreasonable searches and seizures by the government. Some argue that if inspections are required, they should apply equally to all animal-related businesses."Same rule should apply for everybody," Lorna Menaker said, adding she supports broader accountability across the industry."I want to everybody whether its groomers, trainers, rescue — whatever it is, if you're involved with animals, you soul be accountable. There should be some oversight."The proposed ordinance would also require livestock owners to post a county-issued ID number at every entry point, at a cost of $40 per parcel. It would expand rabies tag options and increase incentives for pet microchipping.Staff will review the ordinance before presenting it to county commissioners on Nov. 17.This story was reported onair by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. A nearly 85-acre entertainment district is in the works in Port St. Lucie along Village Parkway in the Tradition community, and developers say new restaurants and stores could arrive sooner than expected.Gustavo Lumer, CEO of Lumer Real Estate, is behind the property that would become the Tradition Entertainment District. WATCH BELOW: New entertainment district planned for Tradition The development is divided between four parcels along Village Parkway from Innovation Way to Hegener Drive.Lumer said he hopes to bring in around 25 new restaurants and additional stores to the area."There's a need for diversity, and they keep telling us that they want different options," Lumer said.Development will start on a 5.5-acre parcel off Innovation Way, which will include 40,000 square feet of retail and restaurant space. Lumer said 60 percent of that space is already leased, and he expects construction to start within six months."The retailers are eager to open yesterday. If we could pop it up next week and have it there, they're ready to go," Lumer said.The next phase will develop 2 parcels totaling around 60 acres farther south, near the new Stars and Stripes Park.Lumer said this section would be the "hub" of the entertainment district.Plans include potentially 15 restaurants, a luxury gym, grocery stores, retail and possibly a movie theater."It'll be a place where you can park or come with your golf cart and spend the afternoon going around different places," Lumer said.Lumer said the district will help keep and attract business in Port St. Lucie."The more brands that they keep opening, everybody's realizing, well, I'm the only one missing out, and so you'll see a lot of beautiful brands coming in a short, short time," Lumer said.Neighbors in the area said they welcome the development. LaVaughn Harvey said he would visit often."I'd be there a lot more," Harvey said.Neighbor Tina Gramata said the district fills a community need."We need more places for people to go on a regular basis to intermingle," Gramata said.Lumer said they are still working on final site approvals for the first parcel off Innovation Way and will begin working on site plan approval for the remaining three sites."That's a lot of retail and a lot of restaurants, and hopefully we can bring entertainment venues," Lumer said.

Barry Melrose, a hockey player-turned-coach who led the Los Angeles Kings to the 1993 Stanley Cup Final before going on to a long career in broadcasting the sport, has died. He was 70.ESPN announced Melrose’s death Wednesday after his wife informed the network.“From the flowing locks of his distinctive mullet to the flared lapels of his trademark long suit coats, Barry Melrose cut an unmistakable figure whenever you were fortunate enough to run into him at a rink or catch him on your television screen," NHL Commissioner Gary Bettman said. “You were even more fortunate if you engaged him in conversation or listened to his analysis because he never failed to boost your love of the game of hockey.”Melrose stepped away from his analyst role in 2023 after being diagnosed with Parkinson’s disease. Wayne Gretzky at the time said Melrose was “bigger than any team.”Melrose had a relatable everyman’s broadcasting style, bringing a sense of humor to his insights, and was easily recognized by his goatee and slicked-backed hair.“For decades, Barry Melrose was one of the most distinctive and trusted voices in hockey," ESPN said in a statement. “His knowledge of the game was deep, his candor was refreshing and his passion was unmistakable.”From rural Kelvington, Saskatchewan, Melrose broke into pro hockey with the Cincinnati Stingers of the now-defunct World Hockey Association in 1976. He played three seasons in Cincinnati — the last teaming with a young Mark Messier — and, following the WHA’s demise, made the transition to the NHL with Winnipeg in 1979.Melrose went on to play for Toronto and Detroit, where he closed his career following the 1985-86 season.He finished with 10 goals and 33 points and 728 penalty minutes in 300 career NHL regular-season games, and he skated in seven more in the playoffs. His WHA totals were five goals and 32 points and 343 penalty minutes in 178 games with Cincinnati.RELATED STORY | ESPN co-founder Bill Rasmussen dies from the effects of Parkinson’s diseaseMelrose turned to coaching and led the Adirondack Red Wings to win the American Hockey League Calder Cup championship in 1992.The following year, Melrose was hired by the Kings, where he brought a sense of colorful flare and instant success to Los Angeles. In his rookie season, he coached a Kings team that featured Gretzky to make a memorable playoff run. They reached the final before losing to Montreal in five games.Melrose finished with a record of 79-101 and 29 ties over two-plus seasons in L.A. before being fired midway through the 1994-95 season.He was hired by ESPN in 1996 and left broadcasting for what became a brief stint coaching the Tampa Bay Lightning in Steven Stamkos’ rookie season in 2008-09. Melrose was fired 16 games into the season following a 5-7-4 start and returned to broadcasting.Melrose also was known for his long-ball hitting prowess in fast-pitch softball, joining fellow Kelvington-area NHL players Wendel Clark, Joey Kocur, Kelly Chase and Kevin Kaminski and others in the offseason in Saskatchewan to form what some call the “the toughest team there ever was.”

LIV Golf, the professional golf league launched in 2022 as a rival to the traditional PGA Tour, filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection Tuesday.In a filing made in the U.S. Bankruptcy Court for the District of New Jersey, LIV Golf said it has reached an agreement with investment firm BC Partners Credit to recapitalize the league, with hopes of transferring majority ownership to its athletes.The move comes just months after Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund (PIF) announced it would stop funding LIV Golf following the 2026 season. PIF had invested more than $5 billion in LIV since its launch, helping to prop up massive player contracts and tournament payouts.RELATED STORY | LIV Golf faces uncertain future as Saudi funding endsAccording to the bankruptcy filing, PIF has agreed to provide nearly $50 million in financing to keep LIV Golf afloat during the bankruptcy proceedings. Once LIV exits bankruptcy, BC Partners and other potential investors are expected to provide additional financing to keep the league operational.LIV Golf CEO Scott O'Neil said the bankruptcy process is intended to create a path toward a new ownership model centered on players and fans."The people of LIV Golf, led by the players, have continued to show incredible resilience, commitment, and a shared belief in what we are building. Thanks to their tireless work, LIV Golf has created a foundation to entertain and inspire the next generation of global golf fans around the world," O'Neil said. "This process gives us the structure and time to pursue a landmark transaction and begin the next chapter of LIV Golf – one built around the fans, an innovative, player-first ownership model, and a part of the global golf ecosystem."IN CASE YOU MISSED IT | Trump’s role as LIV Golf host renews scrutiny over conflicts of interestGene Davis, Chairman of the Board's Special Committee, said protecting what the league has built remains the board's top priority."LIV Golf's players, employees, and business partners have been central to its growth since its founding. In just a few years, they have built a global platform and expanded the game of golf worldwide," Davis said. "The Board's priority is to protect what they have built. Working closely with Scott, management, and expert advisors, we reviewed all available options and believe today's actions reflect the most responsible path forward for the League and its stakeholders."

A new water-management project in Martin County is expected to redirect billions of gallons of water away from the St. Lucie Estuary, helping reduce the risk of harmful algal blooms. Ron DeSantis joined state environmental officials in Palm City on Wednesday to mark the completion of the C-23 Estuary Discharge Diversion Project . The project includes nearly seven miles of new canal and a pump station that will redirect excess water from the C-23 Canal to the C-44 reservoir and stormwater treatment area. There, the water can be stored and cleaned instead of flowing directly into the St. This is yet another tool to manage water before it reaches the estuary, DeSantis said. It will, of course, allow us to further the reduction of harmful discharges and algal blooms within the St. The system entered operational testing in May and has already diverted nearly 5 billion gallons of water, according to DeSantis. Drew Bartlett, executive director of the South Florida Water Management District , said the pump station can move as much as 166 million gallons of water per day. It has worked since May 14, Bartlett said. I looked at the water quality data. Historically, excess water from the C-23 Canal was routed toward the South Fork of the St. Those freshwater flows can disrupt the estuary’s natural salinity balance while carrying nutrients that contribute to algae growth. A more natural salinity gradient and better conditions for the estuary will produce better results for residents, for visitors, for business owners all along the Indian River Lagoon, DeSantis said. Florida Department of Environmental Protection Secretary Alexis Lambert said the completed project is expected to divert 6.3 billion gallons of water from the St. She said it is also projected to prevent an average of 55,000 pounds of nitrogen and 14,000 pounds of phosphorus from entering the river each year. "Projects like this are a lasting investment in the future of our state," Lambert said. Lucie County moves ahead on bulk water agreement for P1 Motor private racetrack club The St. Lucie River and Indian River Lagoon suffered widespread toxic algae outbreaks in 2016 and 2018. The blooms damaged wildlife habitat, hurt local businesses and kept residents away from affected waterways. For Newton Cook, who lives near the Indian River Lagoon, clean water isn't just good for the environment, it's good for the community. "Dirty water, you don't want to live near dirty water," said Cook, who lives in Tequesta. "People want to live near clean water." State officials said the new diversion system should help move conditions in the estuary closer to their natural pattern. While a cleaner estuary will be better for local businesses and people like Cook, he says there's more work to do. "[There's] been a tremendous improvement in the water in different areas but there's still a long way to go," Cook said. The project is part of a broader network of restoration efforts involving the St. Lucie River, Indian River Lagoon and Everglades. The South Florida Water Management District and U.S. Army Corps of Engineers also recently marked the completion of construction on the C-23/C-24 Stormwater Treatment Area , which is designed to remove nutrients from water before it reaches the estuary and southern Indian River Lagoon. DeSantis said Florida has committed nearly $10 billion to Everglades restoration and water-quality projects since he took office in 2019. His administration has completed or begun work on more than 90 Everglades-related projects, he said. The governor also discussed the Everglades Agricultural Area Reservoir south of Lake Okeechobee . DeSantis said a state and federal agreement is expected to accelerate that project’s completion from 2034 to 2029. Once completed, the EAA reservoir is designed to store water from Lake Okeechobee, clean it and send it south toward the Everglades and Florida Bay rather than releasing it east into the St. Lucie River or west into the Caloosahatchee River.

Frank Frangella spent weeks digging through rubble at Ground Zero after the September 11 attacks. Now, he leads safety and security for all Martin County schools — and he hasn’t forgotten a single moment. Frangella’s office serves as a quiet tribute to that day. Photos, statues, and mementos fill the space, each one tied to his time working at Ground Zero in the weeks and months following the attacks. Among them is a memory book, photos of his team, images of mountains of debris and twisted metal, and pictures of celebrities who brought hot meals to first responders. One photo stands out above the rest — filled with circular light reflections that Frangella likes to think of as the ascending souls of those lost that day. For Frangella, the phrase “never forget” carries a meaning that extends well beyond September 11, 2001. “That it happened, that we acknowledge that it happened and the lives that were lost.” Frangella said. “Not only on that day, but for the last 25 years. Everybody else that unfortunately passed away from illnesses of being down there.” Frangella now calls Martin County home. He said he cannot bring himself to return to the 9/11 museum and memorial in New York City, saying it would be too painful. Ex-Fort Pierce officer accused of using Flock database 382 times to track ex-girlfriend The Fort Pierce Police Department announced the arrest of a former officer accused of misusing police database systems.

A former Fort Pierce police officer was arrested after investigators say he accessed Flock and other databases hundreds of times to track his ex-girlfriend. Josepher Crutchfield, who resigned from the Fort Pierce Police Department last month, was arrested Tuesday on four felony counts related to unauthorized computer access, according to the department. He was being held at the St. Lucie County Jail on $80,000 secured bond. Flock cameras are license plate readers law enforcement can use to help identify vehicles connected to suspects in crimes. "The cameras are here for our community's safety, not to be abused by those who are entrusted to safeguarding," said Fort Pierce Police Chief David Smith. Crutchfield had previously faced an Internal Affairs investigation over allegations of sexually inappropriate behavior toward female Fort Pierce police employees in 2021. Investigators said his behavior was excessive, unwelcome, and affected the employees' work environment. The department ultimately found he violated five policies and suspended him for two days without pay. The latest investigation began on Aug. 10, 2026 after the department was contacted by the media about concerns over possible misuse of its Flock automated license plate reader system. Crutchfield was placed on administrative leave on Aug. 7, 2026 and his access to law enforcement systems was revoked. A criminal investigation began Aug. Crutchfield resigned days later on Aug. 18 before the investigation was completed. Investigators later determined there was probable cause for his arrest. Chief Smith called the incident a black eye for the department. "The public places immense trust in those who wear this badge, and with that trust comes a tremendous responsibility. No one is above the law," he said. See also: Details of a Fort Pierce police officer's harassment that got him suspended without pay Between October 2025 and July 2026, Crutchfield allegedly accessed the Flock database 382 times to search the same license plate, using different reason categories and without a legitimate law enforcement purpose. Most of the searches were made while he was off duty. Investigators determined the vehicle was registered to an ex-girlfriend. The investigation expanded to other databases, including FCIC , NCIC , DAVID and TLO . Investigators found Crutchfield made additional searches over the last few years to look up people's names and personal information - searches that they said had no legitimate law enforcement purpose. Those databases contain restricted personal information, including addresses and dates of birth. Officers must acknowledge a warning each time they access the systems, confirming they are being used for legitimate law enforcement purposes. The chief said investigators are not speculating about Crutchfield's intentions or whether the alleged conduct amounted to stalking, but they will follow any additional leads. "The conduct alleged in this case is unacceptable and represents a serious breach of the trust that's placed in law enforcement," Smith said. " Again, it does not diminish the dedicated work that our officers do every day." The department has launched a broader audit of its law enforcement databases. So far, officials said no additional violations have been identified. Fort Pierce police have also tightened access to the Flock system. Only lieutenants and higher ranking officers can now use it, and each search requires approval from one of two deputy chiefs and a case number. Flock searches will be limited to forcible felony investigations and missing or endangered person cases. The department also cut its data retention period from 30 days to seven days. "The system will not be used for general investigative surveillance, intelligence gathering unrelated to an authorized investigation, or routine investigative inquiries," said Smith. Officials also added a position within the Office of Professional Standards to conduct monthly audits of law enforcement databases. The chief acknowledged the incident is a setback for the department but said officials are committed to being transparent and holding officers accountable. "This is a black eye for the agency," the chief said. "This is a difficult moment for our organization and our community, but our responsibility is clear. The authority entrusted to police officers comes with an extraordinary responsibility. When there is criminal evidence that an officer may have violated the law, we have an obligation to act. The badge does not provide immunity from accountability."

Ron DeSantis on Wednesday celebrated the completion of the C-23 Canal Estuary Discharge Diversion Project in Martin County, calling it part of the largest environmental restoration effort in U.S. The project, located at 10297 Southwest Martin Highway, will reroute excess water from the C-23 Canal away from the South Fork of the Saint Lucie River — where it had previously contributed to harmful algal blooms — and instead send it through a nearly 7-mile interconnect canal to the C-44 Reservoir and Stormwater Treatment Area. DeSantis was joined at the ribbon-cutting by Florida Department of Environmental Protection Secretary Alexis Lambert and South Florida Water Management District Executive Director Drew Bartlett, along with district board members Chairman Goss, Ronnie Bergeron, Ben Butler, Charlotte Roman, Tom Hurley and Robert Spotswood Jr. Since entering its operational testing phase in May, the project has diverted nearly 5 billion gallons of water away from the Saint Lucie Estuary. When operating at full capacity, the pump stations can fill an Olympic-size swimming pool in just under 6 minutes. Lambert said the project is projected to prevent 55,000 pounds of nitrogen and 14,000 pounds of phosphorus from entering the Saint Lucie River on average each year, and will divert 6.3 billion gallons of water from the river to the C-44 Reservoir and Stormwater Treatment Area. "Florida's waterways are a deeply interconnected system and preventing these harmful discharges will further improve the health of the estuary and the lagoon," Lambert said. DeSantis said his administration has invested close to $10 billion in Everglades restoration and water quality since taking office in January 2019 — a figure he said has never been matched in state history. He said his administration set an initial funding goal, beat it by nearly $1 billion in his first term, then set a second-term goal of $3.5 billion and has reached nearly $6 billion. The governor said his administration has completed or broken ground on more than 90 Everglades projects and has reached more project milestones than any previous administration in Florida history. He cited reductions of 5.6 million pounds of nitrogen per year and nearly 1 million pounds of phosphorus per year as among the tangible results of those investments. DeSantis also highlighted progress on the Everglades Agricultural Area reservoir south of Lake Okeechobee, which he said was originally scheduled for completion in 2034. Through a partnership with the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers announced after President Donald Trump took office in January 2025, the project is now projected to be completed by 2029 and at nearly half the original federal cost estimate. "Isn't that something — what you want — under budget, ahead of schedule," DeSantis said. The EAA reservoir is designed to store 78 billion gallons of water and deliver 270 billion to 470 billion gallons of clean freshwater each year to the Everglades and Florida Bay. Bartlett said the pump station at the C-23 project site is capable of moving 166 million gallons of water every day — comparable in capacity to Miami's drinking water system — and has been operational since May 14. "We haven't had a lost summer since you've been in office, Governor," Bartlett said. "Have not had a lost summer." Lambert pointed to measurable environmental improvements since DeSantis took office, including seagrass returning to stable levels in the Indian River Lagoon and Saint Lucie Estuary, supporting fish and manatee populations as well as the ecotourism industry. The Indian River Lagoon and Saint Lucie Estuary are home to more than 4,000 species of plant and wildlife. DeSantis said the broader Everglades restoration effort is the largest and most ambitious restoration project in U.S. "When you think about America 250 — a massive country that spans a continent from sea to shining sea — there have been a lot of things that have been done over those 250 years, and there's never been a project of this magnitude that has been attempted, much less brought to fruition like we have," DeSantis said. The trial for Palm City dog trainer and boarder Nikki Camerlengo has been delayed until 2027 — at least the ninth continuance in a case that began more than two years ago. In court Wednesday morning, prosecutor Kristin Chase said one of the state's key witnesses is on medical disability and told Judge Elizabeth Metzger that doctors say she cannot testify until at least the end of January. That witness must first testify at a hearing to determine whether she will be allowed to take the stand at trial. Metzger is now aiming for February for that hearing, pushing any potential trial date even further back. Camerlengo faces two counts of animal cruelty in the deaths of two dogs, deputies say, that died while in the care of her Palm City training and boarding facility, Pawsitively Paradise. She was arrested in 2024 after Martin County detectives said the dogs died in her care. A WPTV investigation linked at least seven dog deaths or serious injuries to Pawsitively Paradise over the course of a decade. Her attorneys are now asking the judge to throw out the case altogether. Court records show the defense, on Sept. 2, filed a motion to dismiss, and Metzger ordered both sides to set a hearing on that motion by the end of this week. Camerlengo's next court date is set for December, though the judge could take up the motion to dismiss sooner. The latest delay comes after a contentious July 2026 hearing in which Metzger pressed both the prosecution and defense over why the case still hadn't gone to trial. "I wanted you here, because I thought I was very clear in the past on what you needed to do," Metzger said at that hearing. "This case has been continued so many times, I've lost count." At one point, an exchange between Metzger and Camerlengo's defense attorney, Stuart Kaplan, grew heated. "Your Honor, it's of no fault of the defendant," Kaplan said. "I'm not saying that," Metzger said. "You're looking at me!" Kaplan said. "I'm not saying that!" Metzger replied. Kaplan has asked the court to block testimony from both the Texas veterinary pathologist who performed the two necropsies and from lead investigator Detective Christine Polizzi. "I think the detective jumped the gun, so to speak. I don't think she had all of the facts," Kaplan told WPTV. The hearing to decide whether those witnesses can testify has not yet taken place. For Adele Kirk Csontos, the wait for justice started even before Camerlengo's arrest. She filed a police report after her dog, Mako, died following 48 hours at Pawsitively Paradise in November 2022. It's probably going to sound crazy, but I literally for two weeks I couldn't talk to my friends," Kirk Csontos said. "I felt responsible." Camerlengo was never charged in Mako's death — his necropsy was inconclusive. Necropsies of two other dogs concluded they died from blunt force trauma, leading to her arrest and charges. "I mean, I know the wheels of justice turn very slowly, but no, I didn't think it would be two years," Kirk Csontos said. Despite the ongoing delays, Kirk Csontos said she has not given up hope. Ron DeSantis on Wednesday celebrated the completion of the C-23 Canal Estuary Discharge Diversion Project in Martin County, calling it part of the largest environmental restoration effort in U.S. The project, located at 10297 Southwest Martin Highway, will reroute excess water from the C-23 Canal away from the South Fork of the Saint Lucie River — where it had previously contributed to harmful algal blooms — and instead send it through a nearly 7-mile interconnect canal to the C-44 Reservoir and Stormwater Treatment Area. DeSantis was joined at the ribbon-cutting by Florida Department of Environmental Protection Secretary Alexis Lambert and South Florida Water Management District Executive Director Drew Bartlett, along with district board members Chairman Goss, Ronnie Bergeron, Ben Butler, Charlotte Roman, Tom Hurley and Robert Spotswood Jr. Since entering its operational testing phase in May, the project has diverted nearly 5 billion gallons of water away from the Saint Lucie Estuary. When operating at full capacity, the pump stations can fill an Olympic-size swimming pool in just under 6 minutes. Lambert said the project is projected to prevent 55,000 pounds of nitrogen and 14,000 pounds of phosphorus from entering the Saint Lucie River on average each year, and will divert 6.3 billion gallons of water from the river to the C-44 Reservoir and Stormwater Treatment Area. "Florida's waterways are a deeply interconnected system and preventing these harmful discharges will further improve the health of the estuary and the lagoon," Lambert said. DeSantis said his administration has invested close to $10 billion in Everglades restoration and water quality since taking office in January 2019 — a figure he said has never been matched in state history. He said his administration set an initial funding goal, beat it by nearly $1 billion in his first term, then set a second-term goal of $3.5 billion and has reached nearly $6 billion. The governor said his administration has completed or broken ground on more than 90 Everglades projects and has reached more project milestones than any previous administration in Florida history. He cited reductions of 5.6 million pounds of nitrogen per year and nearly 1 million pounds of phosphorus per year as among the tangible results of those investments. DeSantis also highlighted progress on the Everglades Agricultural Area reservoir south of Lake Okeechobee, which he said was originally scheduled for completion in 2034. Through a partnership with the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers announced after President Donald Trump took office in January 2025, the project is now projected to be completed by 2029 and at nearly half the original federal cost estimate. "Isn't that something — what you want — under budget, ahead of schedule," DeSantis said. The EAA reservoir is designed to store 78 billion gallons of water and deliver 270 billion to 470 billion gallons of clean freshwater each year to the Everglades and Florida Bay. Bartlett said the pump station at the C-23 project site is capable of moving 166 million gallons of water every day — comparable in capacity to Miami's drinking water system — and has been operational since May 14. "We haven't had a lost summer since you've been in office, Governor," Bartlett said. "Have not had a lost summer." Lambert pointed to measurable environmental improvements since DeSantis took office, including seagrass returning to stable levels in the Indian River Lagoon and Saint Lucie Estuary, supporting fish and manatee populations as well as the ecotourism industry. The Indian River Lagoon and Saint Lucie Estuary are home to more than 4,000 species of plant and wildlife. DeSantis said the broader Everglades restoration effort is the largest and most ambitious restoration project in U.S. "When you think about America 250 — a massive country that spans a continent from sea to shining sea — there have been a lot of things that have been done over those 250 years, and there's never been a project of this magnitude that has been attempted, much less brought to fruition like we have," DeSantis said. About 800 gallons of untreated wastewater spilled from a Port St. Lucie lift station Tuesday after the station lost full electrical power, according to a pollution notice filed with the Florida Department of Environmental Protection. Utility staff discovered sewage escaping from the wet well lid at the WP-22 lift station at 170 SW Hawthorne Circle at about 11 a.m. during weekly station checks, the notice said. The wastewater was flowing onto the station driveway and a nearby swale at an estimated rate of 10 gallons per minute, according to the report. Staff determined the station was not receiving full FPL line power, reported the outage and deployed a backup generator to restart the pumps. The spill stopped at about 12:20 p.m., the report said. City staff estimated about 80 gallons, or 10% of the wastewater, soaked into the soil. A vacuum truck recovered about 720 gallons from the stone surface, grass and swale area, according to the notice. Workers disinfected the affected area with lime. The report said no surface water or public-access areas were affected, and sampling was not required. See also: Former Fort Pierce officer arrested over alleged misuse of police databases The pollution notice said the issue was not detected through the city’s SCADA monitoring system. Regulatory agencies and internal city notifications were underway, according to the report.

After months of delays, public pushback and political debate, West Palm Beach's controversial Downtown Master Plan update is moving forward again — but not without major changes and lingering concerns from residents.During a nearly four-hour Downtown Action Committee meeting, city officials, planners, engineers, residents and neighborhood advocates packed the room — a sharp contrast from earlier discussions.WATCH BELOW: West Palm Beach removes waterfront high-rises from master plan"Those meetings were like ghost towns," said Mike Schmidt, vice president of the Downtown Neighborhood Association. "Now it's like a Taylor Swift press conference."City officials say the Downtown Master Plan update is needed because West Palm Beach is growing rapidly and evolving into a nationally recognized urban center. Leaders say they want to better connect CityPlace and downtown, encourage housing options and guide development in a way that improves quality of life.But residents argue growth is already straining infrastructure and changing the character of the city too quickly."We do not experience development one project at a time — it's all together," said India Foster with the West Palm Beach Residents Coalition.Officials presented data showing downtown growth has actually slowed compared to previous years. Between 2015 and 2025, the city averaged roughly 290 new residential units per year downtown.Still, downtown now contains more than 9,000 residential units, and residents repeatedly questioned whether roads, emergency services and parking can keep up.Traffic dominated much of the discussion.City traffic engineer Saurabh Basnet said some intersections are nearing capacity, especially Okeechobee Boulevard."It's at about 98% capacity," Basnet told the committee.Officials said future improvements could help relieve congestion, including:New road connections such as Fern StreetAdaptive traffic signals that respond to real-time traffic conditionsExpanded Palm Tran serviceSafer walking and biking infrastructureTransportation demand management strategies aimed at reducing vehicle tripsBasnet said if the city does nothing, congestion could significantly worsen by 2045.But many residents said the city's traffic analysis does not reflect reality."Being told traffic is manageable — that is not lived experience," Foster said.Others questioned whether studies account for seasonal residents, construction impacts and future development already in the pipeline.Concerns also came from the West Palm Beach firefighters union, which said taller buildings create unique emergency response challenges. Such as longer wait times due to firefighters needing to climb more stories.Ryan Stacey, speaking on behalf of the firefighters union, said the department is "aggressively neutral" on growth but disappointed the plan does not specifically address first responder needs."If it's on a 25-story building, very different than a short building," he said.He noted the department has added 84 firefighters and a new truck in recent years but said future planning must include police and fire staffing needs as downtown density increases."I think a continued pause is absolutely warranted," he said.The most significant revision to the plan involves the Flagler Waterfront District.An earlier proposal would have allowed buildings up to 25 stories along portions of the waterfront through development incentives. That proposal has now been removed.Under the updated version:Most of Flagler Drive will remain capped at five storiesAreas north of Banyan Boulevard can still allow up to eight stories under existing incentivesTaller development would instead be concentrated farther inland in designated downtown districtsResidents who opposed high-rise waterfront development celebrated the change."This is an important step," said Fatima Sanandaji, co-founder of Save West Palm Beach.Schmidt agreed."What's going on here is showing some of our comments are bearing fruit," he said.Still, some warned that taller buildings just one block west of Flagler could still impact waterfront views and infrastructure.City documents presented to neighborhood groups outlined several additional revisions:Downtown parks along Flagler Drive remain protected as Urban Open SpaceNew large developments must reduce projected vehicle trips by 25%Nonresidential parking requirements south of Banyan Boulevard would be reduced by 20%Residential parking requirements would remain unchangedProjects using development incentives would face stronger workforce housing requirementsWorkforce housing affordability periods would increase from 20 years to 30 yearsDevelopers using city incentives would need to provide more affordable housing or pay city feesA major point of tension emerged over timing.A separate mayor-appointed Neighborhood Partnership Network has spent the last two months researching downtown growth and says it still has hundreds of unanswered questions.Members told the committee they were surprised the process was moving ahead before their recommendations were complete."If there's a group the mayor put together and they are saying wait — what's happening?" asked Downtown Action Committee board member Michael Bakst.Jessica Swift, a member of the partnership group, said volunteers have spent 65 days researching the issue and still need more time."We are volunteers," Swift said. "We have no intention to hold up this process."She said the group has submitted 180 questions to the city and received answers to only seven.Others argued the city is moving too quickly on decisions that could permanently reshape West Palm Beach."Once adopted, West Palm Beach will be changed forever and difficult to reverse," Sanandaji warned.DAC board members emphasized the Downtown Action Committee only serves in an advisory role.The final decisions will be made by the West Palm Beach City Commission.Officials also clarified that if no updates are approved, some existing development incentives from prior plans could still allow high-rise projects along portions of Flagler Drive under current regulations.After lengthy debate, the committee voted to move the recommendations forward.The first reading before city commissioners is expected on Oct. 26, with a final vote anticipated next year.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Less than a year after JetBlue touched down at Vero Beach Regional Airport, the airline is already cutting one of its routes. This comes as JetBlue adds eight new nonstop routes to Fort-lauderdale Hollywood International Airport. A 66-year-old Miami man driving a box truck was killed Monday after the vehicle overturned on Florida’s Turnpike in St. The crash happened near mile marker 166 in unincorporated St. FHP said the truck was traveling north in the outside lane when, for reasons still under investigation, it partially entered the outside paved shoulder before re-entering the travel lanes and overturning, according to Florida Highway Patrol . The truck then collided with a guardrail on the outside shoulder and came to rest on its roof. The driver was pronounced dead at the scene at 9:43 a.m. A 31-year-old Miami man was also inside the truck. FHP said he was flown to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital in Fort Pierce and is listed in stable condition. SLCSO said that due to the crash investigation, both the northbound and southbound lanes of the Turnpike have reopened after being closed for hours at Okeechobee Road. The sheriff's office said motorists should avoid the area and seek alternative routes. "At first, it looked like the driver might have been trying to avoid another vehicle," Delerme said. "It also appeared that he may have fallen asleep, but we cannot say for sure what happened." Delerme and another passenger in the car, Stacey Delgado, said the truck suddenly swerved to the left and then back to the right before the driver lost control. He said the truck flipped twice on the Turnpike before hitting the guardrail, which brought the vehicle to a stop. They said they immediately got out of their vehicle and called 911. When they approached the truck, it was upside down. They saw one unresponsive male and one female who was conscious and responsive inside the vehicle. The woman later confirmed there were only two people in the truck. According to Delerme, the woman was speaking Spanish and saying that a part of her body was hurting. He said they stayed at the scene while emergency responders worked to remove both people from the truck. When they eventually left, responders were still working to remove the unresponsive male and the woman. "This is what we personally saw and heard at the scene," Delerme said. The Florida Highway Patrol is at the scene investigating the circumstances surrounding the crash. SLCSO is assisting with traffic control. The cause of the crash has not yet been determined.

Florida Realtors has a new sales pitch: a property-tax cut.The association is putting $10 million behind Vote Yes on 3, giving supporters of the proposed constitutional amendment a major financial backer after a summer of organized opposition.WATCH BELOW: Florida Realtors puts $10M behind Amendment 3The new campaign centers on a straightforward argument: Buying a home is only part of the affordability challenge. Families also need help paying to keep it."Affordability doesn't end at closing. There's lots of costs that go into homeownership. For example, insurance, repairs, property taxes," said Margy Grant, CEO of Florida Realtors.Amendment 3 would increase the homestead exemption for non-school property taxes to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028, with inflation adjustments afterward. The larger exemption would reduce the value of qualifying homes subject to those taxes.The measure would also lower the annual assessment-growth cap on non-homestead properties, including rentals and commercial buildings, from 10% to 5%. That cap applies to assessed values used to calculate taxes; local tax rates could still change.Grant said the changes would help homeowners retain more of their earnings and give rental and commercial property owners more predictability."Amendment 3 provides the opportunity for homeowners to literally receive money that they've earned and keep more of it," she said.The campaign arrives as Gov. Ron DeSantis has said he will help promote the amendment in some capacity, despite wanting a larger property-tax cut.Opponents argue the promised savings could show up elsewhere on residents' bills."You might pay a couple of thousand dollars less for your property taxes, but you're going to wind up paying more as the cost shifts onto fees, additional assessments," said Edie Ousley, a spokesperson for Vote No on Amendment 3.The state's Revenue Estimating Conference projects that the amendment would eventually reduce annual local, non-school property-tax revenue by about $11.8 billion if approved. The estimated losses begin at roughly $4.93 billion in fiscal year 2027–28 and grow over time.Cities, counties and public-safety groups opposing the amendment warn that those losses could force cuts to services, higher fees or additional assessments."Are you going to have to pay a fee to use your local library? What about fire assessment fees, storm water, additional storm water fees?" Ousley said.Asked about those concerns, Grant said the impact would vary across Florida's 67 counties and expressed confidence that local officials could make decisions to manage it.Both sides now face a campaign to shape how voters understand the measure.An Aug. 18 Sachs Media survey of 800 Florida voters found 63% support overall and 37% opposition. That puts support three percentage points above the 60% required for passage, within the survey's overall margin of error of plus or minus 3.5 percentage points.The survey tested both the original and revised ballot language. Support was 65% among voters shown the revised version and 60% among those shown the original. Pollsters said that difference was not statistically significant.Voters will decide Nov. 3 whether the Realtors' latest pitch closes the deal.

Ron DeSantis on Wednesday celebrated the completion of the C-23 Canal Estuary Discharge Diversion Project in Martin County, calling it part of the largest environmental restoration effort in U.S. The project, located at 10297 Southwest Martin Highway, will reroute excess water from the C-23 Canal away from the South Fork of the Saint Lucie River — where it had previously contributed to harmful algal blooms — and instead send it through a nearly 7-mile interconnect canal to the C-44 Reservoir and Stormwater Treatment Area. DeSantis was joined at the ribbon-cutting by Florida Department of Environmental Protection Secretary Alexis Lambert and South Florida Water Management District Executive Director Drew Bartlett, along with district board members Chairman Goss, Ronnie Bergeron, Ben Butler, Charlotte Roman, Tom Hurley and Robert Spotswood Jr. Since entering its operational testing phase in May, the project has diverted nearly 5 billion gallons of water away from the Saint Lucie Estuary. When operating at full capacity, the pump stations can fill an Olympic-size swimming pool in just under 6 minutes. Lambert said the project is projected to prevent 55,000 pounds of nitrogen and 14,000 pounds of phosphorus from entering the Saint Lucie River on average each year, and will divert 6.3 billion gallons of water from the river to the C-44 Reservoir and Stormwater Treatment Area. "Florida's waterways are a deeply interconnected system and preventing these harmful discharges will further improve the health of the estuary and the lagoon," Lambert said. DeSantis said his administration has invested close to $10 billion in Everglades restoration and water quality since taking office in January 2019 — a figure he said has never been matched in state history. He said his administration set an initial funding goal, beat it by nearly $1 billion in his first term, then set a second-term goal of $3.5 billion and has reached nearly $6 billion. The governor said his administration has completed or broken ground on more than 90 Everglades projects and has reached more project milestones than any previous administration in Florida history. He cited reductions of 5.6 million pounds of nitrogen per year and nearly 1 million pounds of phosphorus per year as among the tangible results of those investments. DeSantis also highlighted progress on the Everglades Agricultural Area reservoir south of Lake Okeechobee, which he said was originally scheduled for completion in 2034. Through a partnership with the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers announced after President Donald Trump took office in January 2025, the project is now projected to be completed by 2029 and at nearly half the original federal cost estimate. "Isn't that something — what you want — under budget, ahead of schedule," DeSantis said. The EAA reservoir is designed to store 78 billion gallons of water and deliver 270 billion to 470 billion gallons of clean freshwater each year to the Everglades and Florida Bay. Bartlett said the pump station at the C-23 project site is capable of moving 166 million gallons of water every day — comparable in capacity to Miami's drinking water system — and has been operational since May 14. "We haven't had a lost summer since you've been in office, Governor," Bartlett said. "Have not had a lost summer." Lambert pointed to measurable environmental improvements since DeSantis took office, including seagrass returning to stable levels in the Indian River Lagoon and Saint Lucie Estuary, supporting fish and manatee populations as well as the ecotourism industry. The Indian River Lagoon and Saint Lucie Estuary are home to more than 4,000 species of plant and wildlife. DeSantis said the broader Everglades restoration effort is the largest and most ambitious restoration project in U.S. "When you think about America 250 — a massive country that spans a continent from sea to shining sea — there have been a lot of things that have been done over those 250 years, and there's never been a project of this magnitude that has been attempted, much less brought to fruition like we have," DeSantis said. One northbound lane of Florida’s Turnpike has reopened in St. Lucie County following a crash that killed a 66-year-old Miami man Sunday morning. Officials said only the left northbound lane is open near mile marker 166 in the Fort Pierce area. Drivers should continue to expect delays as the remaining lanes are closed. The crash was reported at approximately 8:15 a.m., according to the Florida Highway Patrol (FHP). FHP said the 66-year-old man was driving a 2027 Freightliner M2 box truck north in the outside lane when, for reasons still under investigation, the truck partially entered the outside paved shoulder. The truck then re-entered the travel lanes and overturned before hitting a guardrail along the outside shoulder. The truck came to rest on its roof. The driver was pronounced dead at the scene at 9:43 a.m. His identity has not been released, but FHP said his next of kin has been notified. A 31-year-old Miami man who was a passenger in the truck was flown to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital in Fort Pierce. He was listed in stable condition. The rise in diesel prices is putting the squeeze on truck fleets across South Florida. Fort Pierce police officers can no longer run a license plate through the department's Flock camera system on their own. That power now sits with a handful of people at the top of the department, one of several new restrictions Chief David Smith rolled out this week after a former officer was arrested and accused of using the system to search for a woman he once dated 382 times. "The cameras are here for our community's safety, not to be abused by those who were entrusted to safeguard them," Smith said. Under the new rules, every use of the license plate reader system requires sign off from one of the department's two deputy chiefs before a search is run. Only lieutenants and above can access the system at all. Every query must be tied to a case number, and the system can only be used in two situations: investigations of forcible felonies as defined under Florida law, and cases involving missing or endangered people. "The system will not be used for general investigative surveillance, intelligence gathering unrelated to an authorized investigation, or routine investigative inquiries," Smith said. See also: Argument ends in stabbing; victim flees to West Palm Beach fire station, attacked again The department is also holding onto far less of the data it collects. Smith said Flock camera records are now deleted after 7 days instead of 30. Smith laid out how the process works on the ground. If detectives at a shooting or other serious scene believe the cameras could help, the lieutenant on scene calls one of the two deputy chiefs and explains what they want to search and why. "If they receive approval, then that lieutenant would be the one to do the query for that information. And that would require a case number specifically tied to an investigation," Smith said. Before this change, individual officers and detectives had their own user access and could search the system directly. Smith also created a new position in the department's Office of Professional Standards to conduct monthly quality assurance audits of every law enforcement database officers use, not just Flock. "Accountability requires meaningful controls, supervision, and verification," Smith said. While some people who spoke to CBS12 News are happy about the changes, some say they're conflicted about Flock camera use at all. You know, we do have we do have our own rights, you know, and all this data collection and everything else is definitely infringing upon that. On the other side of it, it is a great tool for law enforcement," said Edward Smith. "I think it's a good thing that they crack down on it. Like, you don't have to have it. You know, I don't need a camera watching me walk into the bathroom." Smith said he started reviewing the department's technology policies after becoming chief in February and had already begun a one-year audit of database usage before the media brought the allegations against former officer Josepher Crutchfield to the department in August. But he said the deputy chief approval and lieutenant-only access rules were added after that investigation began. Smith declined to give a specific date for when the earlier changes took effect, saying it was roughly two months ago. "This case demonstrates that the safeguards that were in place were not sufficient," Smith said. "What we learned through this investigation reinforced the need for the changes that were already underway, and it made clear that we needed to go significantly further, and we have." Crutchfield was arrested Tuesday on four felony counts of unauthorized computer access and was being held at the St. Lucie County Jail on an $80,000 bond. Police say he searched the same license plate 382 times between October 2025 and July 2026, most of the time while off duty, and that the plate belonged to a woman he had dated. Investigators say he also searched for her in the FCIC, NCIC, DAVID and TLO databases, some of that going back to 2023. He resigned in August before the investigation concluded. When asked whether that many searches on a single plate should have raised alarms sooner, Smith said the department's audit was already working backward month by month when the media tip came in. "It's definitely unusual activity when you've got somebody doing multiple single point searches on a license plate," Smith said. "I do believe that we would have gotten there and we would have identified these." The department's broader audit is still ongoing. Smith said no additional violations have been found so far. The new rules land as Fort Pierce is also pulling cameras off the road. Smith said the department will comply with a recent Florida Department of Transportation directive and the St. Lucie County Commission's directive covering license plate readers on state and county rights-of-way. He estimated about 50 cameras will come down, leaving roughly 20 on city roads. He said the department is still working on a removal plan and it will take time. Smith defended the technology even as he restricted it, saying the cameras were integral to solving every homicide the city has closed recently and to identifying the driver in the hit-and-run that seriously injured a seven-year-old girl. I understand why people are having that discussion about the use of Flock systems. But it is an immensely useful tool to law enforcement," Smith said.

Frank Frangella spent weeks digging through rubble at Ground Zero after the September 11 attacks. Now, he leads safety and security for all Martin County schools — and he hasn’t forgotten a single moment. Frangella’s office serves as a quiet tribute to that day. Photos, statues, and mementos fill the space, each one tied to his time working at Ground Zero in the weeks and months following the attacks. Among them is a memory book, photos of his team, images of mountains of debris and twisted metal, and pictures of celebrities who brought hot meals to first responders. One photo stands out above the rest — filled with circular light reflections that Frangella likes to think of as the ascending souls of those lost that day. For Frangella, the phrase “never forget” carries a meaning that extends well beyond September 11, 2001. “That it happened, that we acknowledge that it happened and the lives that were lost.” Frangella said. “Not only on that day, but for the last 25 years. Everybody else that unfortunately passed away from illnesses of being down there.” Frangella now calls Martin County home. He said he cannot bring himself to return to the 9/11 museum and memorial in New York City, saying it would be too painful.
