hero.headline: Martin County C-23 Canal project completed, diverts nearly 5 billion gallons
hero.body:
The C-23 Canal Estuary Discharge Diversion Project in Martin County has been completed and is now diverting excess water away from the South Fork of the Saint Lucie River. Since entering its operational testing phase in May, the project has diverted nearly 5 billion gallons of water away from the Saint Lucie Estuary. Florida Department of Environmental Protection Secretary Alexis Lambert said the project is projected to prevent 55,000 pounds of nitrogen and 14,000 pounds of phosphorus from entering the Saint Lucie River on average each year and will divert 6.3 billion gallons of water from the river to the C-44 Reservoir and Stormwater Treatment Area.

Gov. Ron DeSantis celebrated the completion Wednesday at the project site at 10297 Southwest Martin Highway. The project reroutes water from the C-23 Canal through a nearly 7-mile interconnect canal to the C-44 Reservoir and Stormwater Treatment Area instead of sending it to the South Fork of the Saint Lucie River, where it had previously contributed to harmful algal blooms. DeSantis was joined at the ribbon-cutting by Lambert and South Florida Water Management District Executive Director Drew Bartlett, along with district board members Chairman Goss, Ronnie Bergeron, Ben Butler, Charlotte Roman, Tom Hurley and Robert Spotswood Jr.

Bartlett said the pump station at the project site is capable of moving 166 million gallons of water every day and has been operational since May 14. When operating at full capacity, the pump stations can fill an Olympic-size swimming pool in just under 6 minutes. Lambert said the project is part of a deeply interconnected system and preventing harmful discharges will further improve the health of the estuary and the lagoon. She pointed to measurable environmental improvements since DeSantis took office, including seagrass returning to stable levels in the Indian River Lagoon and Saint Lucie Estuary, supporting fish and manatee populations as well as the ecotourism industry.

DeSantis said his administration has invested close to $10 billion in Everglades restoration and water quality since taking office in January 2019 and has completed or broken ground on more than 90 Everglades projects. He highlighted progress on the Everglades Agricultural Area reservoir south of Lake Okeechobee, which was originally scheduled for completion in 2034. Through a partnership with the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers announced after President Donald Trump took office in January 2025, the project is now projected to be completed by 2029 and at nearly half the original federal cost estimate. The EAA reservoir is designed to store 78 billion gallons of water and deliver 270 billion to 470 billion gallons of clean freshwater each year to the Everglades and Florida Bay.

Members of the Carefree Boat Club of the Treasure Coast received a similar email saying that club is also ceasing operations.

The original founder of Carefree Clubs of St. Augustine and Amelia Island sent members an email asking them to take a survey about whether the founder should step back in and rebuild the club.

hero.headline: Fort Pierce police restrict Flock camera access after stalking case
hero.body:
Fort Pierce police officers can no longer run a license plate through the department's Flock camera system on their own. Chief David Smith rolled out sweeping new restrictions this week that require deputy chief approval before every search and limit system access to lieutenants and above. The changes come after former officer Josepher Crutchfield was arrested and accused of using the system to search for a woman he once dated 382 times.

Under the new rules, every use of the license plate reader system requires sign off from one of the department's two deputy chiefs before a search is run. Only lieutenants and above can access the system at all. Every query must be tied to a case number, and the system can only be used in two situations: investigations of forcible felonies as defined under Florida law, and cases involving missing or endangered people. Before this change, individual officers and detectives had their own user access and could search the system directly.

The department is also holding onto far less of the data it collects. Smith said Flock camera records are now deleted after 7 days instead of 30. Smith also created a new position in the department's Office of Professional Standards to conduct monthly quality assurance audits of every law enforcement database officers use, not just Flock. The deputy chief approval and lieutenant-only access rules were added after the investigation into Crutchfield began, Smith said.

Crutchfield was arrested Tuesday on four felony counts of unauthorized computer access and was being held at the St. Lucie County Jail on an $80,000 bond. Police say he searched the same license plate 382 times between October 2025 and July 2026, most of the time while off duty, and that the plate belonged to a woman he had dated. Investigators say he also searched for her in the FCIC, NCIC, DAVID and TLO databases, some of that going back to 2023. He resigned in August before the investigation concluded.

The new rules land as Fort Pierce is also pulling cameras off the road. Smith said the department will comply with a recent Florida Department of Transportation directive and the St. Lucie County Commission's directive covering license plate readers on state and county rights-of-way. He estimated about 50 cameras will come down, leaving roughly 20 on city roads. Smith started reviewing the department's technology policies after becoming chief in February and had already begun a one-year audit of database usage before the media brought the allegations against Crutchfield to the department in August.
hero.article_text: Fort Pierce police officers can no longer run a license plate through the department's Flock camera system on their own. That power now sits with a handful of people at the top of the department, one of several new restrictions Chief David Smith rolled out this week after a former officer was arrested and accused of using the system to search for a woman he once dated 382 times. "The cameras are here for our community's safety, not to be abused by those who were entrusted to safeguard them," Smith said. Under the new rules, every use of the license plate reader system requires sign off from one of the department's two deputy chiefs before a search is run. Only lieutenants and above can access the system at all. Every query must be tied to a case number, and the system can only be used in two situations: investigations of forcible felonies as defined under Florida law, and cases involving missing or endangered people. "The system will not be used for general investigative surveillance, intelligence gathering unrelated to an authorized investigation, or routine investigative inquiries," Smith said. See also: Argument ends in stabbing; victim flees to West Palm Beach fire station, attacked again The department is also holding onto far less of the data it collects. Smith said Flock camera records are now deleted after 7 days instead of 30. Smith laid out how the process works on the ground. If detectives at a shooting or other serious scene believe the cameras could help, the lieutenant on scene calls one of the two deputy chiefs and explains what they want to search and why. "If they receive approval, then that lieutenant would be the one to do the query for that information. And that would require a case number specifically tied to an investigation," Smith said. Before this change, individual officers and detectives had their own user access and could search the system directly. Smith also created a new position in the department's Office of Professional Standards to conduct monthly quality assurance audits of every law enforcement database officers use, not just Flock. "Accountability requires meaningful controls, supervision, and verification," Smith said. While some people who spoke to CBS12 News are happy about the changes, some say they're conflicted about Flock camera use at all. You know, we do have we do have our own rights, you know, and all this data collection and everything else is definitely infringing upon that. On the other side of it, it is a great tool for law enforcement," said Edward Smith. "I think it's a good thing that they crack down on it. Like, you don't have to have it. You know, I don't need a camera watching me walk into the bathroom." Smith said he started reviewing the department's technology policies after becoming chief in February and had already begun a one-year audit of database usage before the media brought the allegations against former officer Josepher Crutchfield to the department in August. But he said the deputy chief approval and lieutenant-only access rules were added after that investigation began. Smith declined to give a specific date for when the earlier changes took effect, saying it was roughly two months ago. "This case demonstrates that the safeguards that were in place were not sufficient," Smith said. "What we learned through this investigation reinforced the need for the changes that were already underway, and it made clear that we needed to go significantly further, and we have." Crutchfield was arrested Tuesday on four felony counts of unauthorized computer access and was being held at the St. Lucie County Jail on an $80,000 bond. Police say he searched the same license plate 382 times between October 2025 and July 2026, most of the time while off duty, and that the plate belonged to a woman he had dated. Investigators say he also searched for her in the FCIC, NCIC, DAVID and TLO databases, some of that going back to 2023. He resigned in August before the investigation concluded. When asked whether that many searches on a single plate should have raised alarms sooner, Smith said the department's audit was already working backward month by month when the media tip came in. "It's definitely unusual activity when you've got somebody doing multiple single point searches on a license plate," Smith said. "I do believe that we would have gotten there and we would have identified these." The department's broader audit is still ongoing. Smith said no additional violations have been found so far. The new rules land as Fort Pierce is also pulling cameras off the road. Smith said the department will comply with a recent Florida Department of Transportation directive and the St. Lucie County Commission's directive covering license plate readers on state and county rights-of-way. He estimated about 50 cameras will come down, leaving roughly 20 on city roads. He said the department is still working on a removal plan and it will take time. Smith defended the technology even as he restricted it, saying the cameras were integral to solving every homicide the city has closed recently and to identifying the driver in the hit-and-run that seriously injured a seven-year-old girl. I understand why people are having that discussion about the use of Flock systems. But it is an immensely useful tool to law enforcement," Smith said.

hero.headline: K-9 Tobi alerts deputies to heroin, marijuana in Indian River County traffic stop
hero.body:
A traffic stop for a minor violation in Indian River County led to drug charges after a police dog detected narcotics in the vehicle, according to the sheriff's office.

Sheriff's office road patrol deputies pulled over a vehicle Sunday night for a minor traffic infraction. K-9 Tobi was brought to the scene and alerted to the presence of drugs. Deputies discovered the vehicle had more than just the illegal window tint that prompted the initial stop.

Substances that appeared to be marijuana tested positive for heroin as well, according to authorities. Jean Baptiste was taken into custody and faces multiple charges, including possession with intent to sell.

The sheriff's office praised the work of the deputies and K-9 Tobi in a Facebook post, saying they did great work keeping the streets safe at night.

cards.headline: Judge denies bond reduction for ex-Fort Pierce officer accused of tracking ex-girlfriend
cards.teaser: A judge denied a request to lower the $80,000 bond for Josepher Crutchfield, who faces four felony counts for allegedly using law enforcement databases to track his ex-girlfriend more than 400 times.
cards.body:
A judge denied a bond reduction request this morning for a former Fort Pierce police officer accused of misusing law enforcement databases to track his ex-girlfriend, keeping his bond at $80,000. Josepher Crutchfield appeared at his first court appearance facing four third-degree felony counts, each carrying a $20,000 warrant.

Crutchfield's attorney asked the judge to reduce his bond, but the state argued the bond should remain in place, citing concerns about public trust in Flock cameras, a tool used by law enforcement to track vehicles. An assistant state attorney told the court that law enforcement officers entrusted with these duties should be the first not to abuse them, particularly given national concerns about Flock cameras.

Police said Crutchfield used Flock cameras and other law enforcement databases more than 400 times to track his ex-girlfriend's car, with 382 of those searches conducted through Flock cameras. Authorities said most of the searches occurred while Crutchfield was off duty, allowing him to see where and when her car was spotted.

Crutchfield resigned from the Fort Pierce Police Department last month after learning he was under investigation. His bond remains set at $80,000.
cards.article_text: A former Fort Pierce police officer accused of misusing law enforcement databases to track his ex-girlfriend appeared in court this morning, where a judge denied his request to lower his $80,000 bond. Josepher Crutchfield, who resigned from the Fort Pierce Police Department last month after learning he was under investigation, is facing four third-degree felony counts, each carrying a $20,000 warrant. Crutchfield’s attorney asked the judge to reduce his bond, but the request was denied. The state argued that the bond should remain in place, citing concerns about trust in Flock cameras, a tool used by law enforcement to track vehicles. "With the national issue with Flock cameras and people's concern about them, law enforcement who's entrusted with these duties should be at least the first people to not abuse them, so I would ask that the bonds of $20,000 on each stay the same," an assistant state attorney said. Police said Crutchfield used Flock cameras and other law enforcement databases more than 400 times to track his ex-girlfriend’s car, with 382 of those searches conducted through Flock cameras. Authorities said most of the searches occurred while Crutchfield was off duty, allowing him to see where and when her car was spotted. Crutchfield made his first court appearance this morning, and his bond remains set at $80,000. cards.headline: Tradition Entertainment District in Port St. Lucie 60% pre-leased, construction to start within six months
cards.teaser: The first phase of the 85-acre Tradition Entertainment District along Village Parkway is 60 percent pre-leased and could begin construction within six months, with a larger entertainment hub planned near Stars and Stripes Park.
cards.body:
The nearly 85-acre Tradition Entertainment District planned along Village Parkway in Port St. Lucie has pre-leased 60 percent of its first retail and restaurant parcel, with construction expected to start within six months, according to developer Gustavo Lumer.

Lumer, CEO of Lumer Real Estate, said the initial development will cover a 5.5-acre parcel off Innovation Way and will include 40,000 square feet of retail and restaurant space. The development is divided among four parcels along Village Parkway from Innovation Way to Hegener Drive.

Lumer said he plans to bring around 25 new restaurants and additional stores to the area. The second phase will develop two parcels totaling around 60 acres farther south, near the new Stars and Stripes Park. Lumer said this section would be the hub of the entertainment district, with plans for potentially 15 restaurants, a luxury gym, grocery stores, retail and possibly a movie theater.

Lumer said retailers are eager to open as soon as possible. Neighbors in the area welcomed the development. LaVaughn Harvey said he would visit often, while neighbor Tina Gramata said the district fills a community need for places where people can intermingle on a regular basis. Lumer said the development team is still working on final site approvals for the first parcel off Innovation Way and will begin working on site plan approval for the remaining three sites.

hero.headline: Nearly 7-mile canal system in Palm City now diverts billions of gallons from St. Lucie Estuary
hero.body:
A new water-management project in Palm City is redirecting billions of gallons of water away from the St. Lucie Estuary to reduce the risk of harmful algal blooms in Martin County. The C-23 Estuary Discharge Diversion Project, which includes nearly seven miles of new canal and a pump station, entered operational testing in May and has already diverted nearly 5 billion gallons of water. The system is projected to prevent an average of 55,000 pounds of nitrogen and 14,000 pounds of phosphorus from entering the river each year.

Ron DeSantis joined state environmental officials in Palm City on Wednesday to mark the completion of the project. The pump station redirects excess water from the C-23 Canal to the C-44 reservoir and stormwater treatment area, where the water can be stored and cleaned instead of flowing directly into the St. Lucie Estuary. Drew Bartlett, executive director of the South Florida Water Management District, said the pump station can move as much as 166 million gallons of water per day.

Historically, excess water from the C-23 Canal was routed toward the South Fork of the St. Lucie River. Those freshwater flows can disrupt the estuary's natural salinity balance while carrying nutrients that contribute to algae growth. Florida Department of Environmental Protection Secretary Alexis Lambert said the completed project is expected to divert 6.3 billion gallons of water from the St. Lucie River.

The St. Lucie River and Indian River Lagoon suffered widespread toxic algae outbreaks in 2016 and 2018. The blooms damaged wildlife habitat, hurt local businesses and kept residents away from affected waterways. DeSantis said a more natural salinity gradient and better conditions for the estuary will produce better results for residents, for visitors, and for business owners all along the Indian River Lagoon.

The project is part of a broader network of restoration efforts involving the St. Lucie River, Indian River Lagoon and Everglades. The South Florida Water Management District and U.S. Army Corps of Engineers also recently marked the completion of construction on the C-23/C-24 Stormwater Treatment Area, which is designed to remove nutrients from water before it reaches the estuary and southern Indian River Lagoon. DeSantis said Florida has committed nearly $10 billion to Everglades restoration and water-quality projects since he took office in 2019.

cards.headline: Palm City dog trainer Nikki Camerlengo's animal cruelty trial delayed to 2027
cards.teaser: The trial for Palm City dog trainer Nikki Camerlengo has been pushed to 2027 after at least a ninth continuance, with a key state witness on medical disability unable to testify until late January. The defense has also filed a motion to dismiss the case entirely.
cards.body:
The trial for Palm City dog trainer and boarder Nikki Camerlengo has been delayed until 2027, marking at least the ninth continuance in a case that began more than two years ago. In court Wednesday morning, prosecutor Kristin Chase told Judge Elizabeth Metzger that one of the state's key witnesses is on medical disability and cannot testify until at least the end of January, according to doctors. That witness must first testify at a hearing to determine whether she will be allowed to take the stand at trial. Metzger is now aiming for February for that hearing, pushing any potential trial date even further back.

Camerlengo faces two counts of animal cruelty in the deaths of two dogs that died while in the care of her Palm City training and boarding facility, Pawsitively Paradise. She was arrested in 2024 after Martin County detectives said the dogs died in her care. A WPTV investigation linked at least seven dog deaths or serious injuries to Pawsitively Paradise over the course of a decade.

Her attorneys filed a motion to dismiss the case on Sept. 2, and Metzger ordered both sides to set a hearing on that motion by the end of this week. Camerlengo's next court date is set for December, though the judge could take up the motion to dismiss sooner. Defense attorney Stuart Kaplan has asked the court to block testimony from both the Texas veterinary pathologist who performed the two necropsies and from lead investigator Detective Christine Polizzi. Kaplan told WPTV he believes the detective did not have all of the facts. The hearing to decide whether those witnesses can testify has not yet taken place.

The latest delay comes after a contentious July 2026 hearing in which Metzger pressed both the prosecution and defense over why the case still hadn't gone to trial. At one point, an exchange between Metzger and Kaplan grew heated. At that hearing, Metzger said the case had been continued so many times she had lost count.

For Adele Kirk Csontos, the wait for justice started even before Camerlengo's arrest. She filed a police report after her dog, Mako, died following 48 hours at Pawsitively Paradise in November 2022. Camerlengo was never charged in Mako's death because his necropsy was inconclusive. Necropsies of two other dogs concluded they died from blunt force trauma, leading to her arrest and charges. Kirk Csontos said she did not think it would be two years. Despite the ongoing delays, Kirk Csontos said she is still hopeful that Camerlengo will be held accountable.

hero.headline: C-23 Canal diversion project in Martin County complete, rerouting billions of gallons from St. Lucie Estuary
hero.body:
Gov. Ron DeSantis on Wednesday celebrated the completion of the C-23 Canal Estuary Discharge Diversion Project in Martin County, calling it part of the largest environmental restoration effort in U.S. history. The project will reroute excess water from the C-23 Canal away from the South Fork of the Saint Lucie River and send it through a nearly 7-mile interconnect canal to the C-44 Reservoir and Stormwater Treatment Area.

Since entering its operational testing phase in May, the project has diverted nearly 5 billion gallons of water away from the Saint Lucie Estuary. The pump station is capable of moving 166 million gallons of water every day and has been operational since May 14. When operating at full capacity, the pump stations can fill an Olympic-size swimming pool in just under 6 minutes.

Florida Department of Environmental Protection Secretary Alexis Lambert said the project is projected to prevent 55,000 pounds of nitrogen and 14,000 pounds of phosphorus from entering the Saint Lucie River on average each year, and will divert 6.3 billion gallons of water from the river to the C-44 Reservoir and Stormwater Treatment Area. The project is located at 10297 Southwest Martin Highway and addresses excess water that had previously contributed to harmful algal blooms in the river.

DeSantis said his administration has invested close to $10 billion in Everglades restoration and water quality since taking office in January 2019. He said his administration has completed or broken ground on more than 90 Everglades projects and cited reductions of 5.6 million pounds of nitrogen per year and nearly 1 million pounds of phosphorus per year as among the tangible results of those investments.

DeSantis was joined at the ribbon-cutting by Lambert and South Florida Water Management District Executive Director Drew Bartlett, along with district board members Chairman Goss, Ronnie Bergeron, Ben Butler, Charlotte Roman, Tom Hurley and Robert Spotswood Jr. Lambert pointed to measurable environmental improvements since DeSantis took office, including seagrass returning to stable levels in the Indian River Lagoon and Saint Lucie Estuary, supporting fish and manatee populations as well as the ecotourism industry.

cards.headline: Florida Realtors puts $10 million behind Amendment 3 property-tax cuts
cards.teaser: Florida Realtors is funding a $10 million campaign to support Amendment 3, which would increase the homestead exemption for non-school property taxes to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028. The state projects the amendment would eventually reduce annual local, non-school property-tax revenue by about $11.8 billion.
cards.body:
Florida Realtors is putting $10 million behind a campaign to pass Amendment 3, which would increase the homestead exemption for non-school property taxes to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028, with inflation adjustments afterward. The measure would also lower the annual assessment-growth cap on non-homestead properties, including rentals and commercial buildings, from 10% to 5%.

Margy Grant, CEO of Florida Realtors, said the changes would help homeowners retain more of their earnings. The campaign centers on the argument that buying a home is only part of the affordability challenge and families need help paying to keep it. Grant said Amendment 3 provides the opportunity for homeowners to receive money they have earned and keep more of it.

The state's Revenue Estimating Conference projects that the amendment would eventually reduce annual local, non-school property-tax revenue by about $11.8 billion if approved. The estimated losses begin at roughly $4.93 billion in fiscal year 2027–28 and grow over time. Edie Ousley, a spokesperson for Vote No on Amendment 3, warned that residents might pay a couple of thousand dollars less for property taxes but wind up paying more as costs shift onto fees and additional assessments. Cities, counties and public-safety groups opposing the amendment warn that losses could force cuts to services, higher fees or additional assessments.

An Aug. 18 Sachs Media survey of 800 Florida voters found 63% support overall and 37% opposition. That puts support three percentage points above the 60% required for passage, within the survey's overall margin of error of plus or minus 3.5 percentage points. Gov. Ron DeSantis has said he will help promote the amendment in some capacity, despite wanting a larger property-tax cut. Voters will decide Nov. 3.

hero.headline: Fort Pierce police restrict Flock camera access to top brass after Crutchfield arrest
hero.body:
Fort Pierce police officers can no longer search license plates through the department's Flock camera system without approval from one of two deputy chiefs, and only lieutenants and above may access the system at all. Chief David Smith announced the restrictions this week after the arrest of former officer Josepher Crutchfield, who is accused of searching for a woman he once dated 382 times through the system.

Under the new rules, every search requires a case number and deputy chief sign off. The system may be used only for investigations of forcible felonies as defined under Florida law and cases involving missing or endangered people. Smith also cut data retention from 30 days to seven days. Before the changes, individual officers and detectives had their own user access and could search the system directly.

Smith created a new position in the department's Office of Professional Standards to conduct monthly audits of every law enforcement database officers use. He said he began reviewing technology policies after becoming chief in February and had already started a one-year audit of database usage before media brought the allegations against Crutchfield to the department in August. The deputy chief approval and lieutenant-only access rules were added after that investigation began, roughly two months ago.

Crutchfield was arrested Tuesday on four felony counts of unauthorized computer access and was being held at the St. Lucie County Jail on an $80,000 bond. Police say he searched the same license plate 382 times between October 2025 and July 2026, most of the time while off duty, and that the plate belonged to a woman he had dated. Investigators say he also searched for her in the FCIC, NCIC, DAVID and TLO databases, some of that going back to 2023. He resigned in August before the investigation concluded.

The new rules arrive as Fort Pierce is also removing cameras from the road. Smith said the department will comply with a recent Florida Department of Transportation directive and the St. Lucie County Commission's directive covering license plate readers on state and county rights of way. He estimated about 50 cameras will come down, leaving roughly 20 on city roads. Smith said the cameras were integral to solving every homicide the city has closed recently and to identifying the driver in the hit and run that seriously injured a seven year old girl.

hero.headline: Martin County C-23 Canal project diverts nearly 5 billion gallons from Saint Lucie Estuary
hero.body:
The C-23 Canal Estuary Discharge Diversion Project in Martin County has diverted nearly 5 billion gallons of water away from the Saint Lucie Estuary since entering its operational testing phase in May. Gov. Ron DeSantis celebrated completion of the project on Wednesday at the site on Southwest Martin Highway.

The project is projected to prevent 55,000 pounds of nitrogen and 14,000 pounds of phosphorus from entering the Saint Lucie River on average each year, according to Florida Department of Environmental Protection Secretary Alexis Lambert. The pump station can move 166 million gallons of water every day and has been operational since May 14.

The project reroutes excess water from the C-23 Canal away from the South Fork of the Saint Lucie River through a nearly 7-mile interconnect canal to the C-44 Reservoir and Stormwater Treatment Area. The water previously contributed to harmful algal blooms in the estuary. When operating at full capacity, the pump stations can fill an Olympic-size swimming pool in just under 6 minutes.

Lambert said the project will divert 6.3 billion gallons of water from the river to the C-44 Reservoir and Stormwater Treatment Area. DeSantis was joined at the ribbon-cutting by Lambert, South Florida Water Management District Executive Director Drew Bartlett, and district board members including Chairman Goss, Ronnie Bergeron, Ben Butler, Charlotte Roman, Tom Hurley and Robert Spotswood Jr.

DeSantis said his administration has invested close to $10 billion in Everglades restoration and water quality since taking office in January 2019. He said his administration has completed or broken ground on more than 90 Everglades projects and has reached more project milestones than any previous administration in Florida history. The governor cited reductions of 5.6 million pounds of nitrogen per year and nearly 1 million pounds of phosphorus per year as among the tangible results of those investments.

Lambert pointed to measurable environmental improvements since DeSantis took office, including seagrass returning to stable levels in the Indian River Lagoon and Saint Lucie Estuary. The Indian River Lagoon and Saint Lucie Estuary are home to more than 4,000 species of plant and wildlife.

hero.headline: Tradition Entertainment District in Port St. Lucie to break ground within six months
hero.body:
Construction on the first phase of the Tradition Entertainment District in Port St. Lucie is expected to begin within six months, with 60 percent of the initial 40,000 square feet of retail and restaurant space already leased. The nearly 85-acre development along Village Parkway in the Tradition community is moving forward faster than anticipated, according to developer Gustavo Lumer, CEO of Lumer Real Estate.

The entertainment district is divided between four parcels along Village Parkway from Innovation Way to Hegener Drive. Development will start on a 5.5-acre parcel off Innovation Way, which will include the 40,000 square feet of retail and restaurant space. Lumer said the retailers are eager to open as soon as possible.

Lumer plans to bring around 25 new restaurants and additional stores to the area. The next phase will develop two parcels totaling around 60 acres farther south, near the new Stars and Stripes Park. This section would serve as the hub of the entertainment district and includes plans for potentially 15 restaurants, a luxury gym, grocery stores, retail and possibly a movie theater.

Lumer said the district will be a place where residents can park or arrive by golf cart and spend the afternoon visiting different establishments. Neighbors in the area have welcomed the development. LaVaughn Harvey said he would visit often, while neighbor Tina Gramata said the district fills a community need for places where people can gather regularly. Lumer said developers are still working on final site approvals for the first parcel off Innovation Way and will begin working on site plan approval for the remaining three sites.

hero.headline: Fort Pierce police restrict Flock camera access after ex-officer's 382 searches
hero.body:

Investigators say he also searched for her in the FCIC, NCIC, DAVID and TLO databases, some of that going back to 2023. He resigned in August before the investigation concluded.

But he said the deputy chief approval and lieutenant-only access rules were added after that investigation began.

Under the new process, if detectives at a shooting or other serious scene believe the cameras could help, the lieutenant on scene calls one of the two deputy chiefs and explains what they want to search and why. If they receive approval, the lieutenant conducts the query using a case number specifically tied to an investigation.

"The system will not be used for general investigative surveillance, intelligence gathering unrelated to an authorized investigation, or routine investigative inquiries," Smith said.

Smith also created a new position in the department's Office of Professional Standards to conduct monthly quality assurance audits of every law enforcement database officers use. The department's broader audit is still ongoing. Smith said no additional violations have been found so far.

The department is also pulling cameras off the road in response to a recent Florida Department of Transportation directive and the St. Lucie County Commission's directive covering license plate readers on state and county rights of way. Smith estimated about 50 cameras will come down, leaving roughly 20 on city roads.
